summary: Examine the shoulder, elbow, wrist and hand, hip, knee, ankle and foot with 55 special tests: position, method, what is positive, what it suggests, the pitfalls and how far to trust it — plus clusters, the Ottawa rules and when to refer.
ur: Shoulder, elbow, wrist, hip, knee aur ankle ke 55 special tests: position, tareeqa, positive finding ka matlab, ghaltiyan aur test par kitna bharosa karna hai — saath mein clusters, Ottawa rules aur kab refer karna hai.

goals.beginner: Know what each test is looking for and what a positive means.
goals.intermediate: Perform each test in the right position, with the right hold and the right force.
goals.advanced: Avoid false results, combine tests and judge the timing.
goals.expert: Turn findings into a decision, including when to image or refer.

concepts.title: What a special test can and cannot do
concepts.body: A special test is a question you ask a joint. It changes how likely a diagnosis is, but it does not make the diagnosis. A single test is rarely enough: the history, the pattern of movement and a small group of tests together give the answer.
bullets: Start with the history: where, when, what movement, and what the patient fears.
Choose a test because it answers a question, not because it is on a list.
Say out loud what a positive and a negative mean before you do the test.
Write the result as the side, the test, what you found, and the pain.
concepts.ur: Special test jod se poochha gaya ek sawal hai. Yeh diagnosis ke chance ko badhata ya ghatata hai, lekin diagnosis khud nahi karta. Sirf ek test aksar kaafi nahi hota: history, harkat ka pattern aur chhote se tests ka group mil kar jawab dete hain. Pehle history lein, test tabhi karein jab usse sawal ka jawab milna ho, aur test se pehle sochein ke positive aur negative ka kya matlab hoga.

concepts.title: Sensitivity, specificity and likelihood ratios
concepts.body: Sensitivity is how often a test is positive in people who have the problem. Specificity is how often it is negative in people who do not. A very sensitive test, when negative, helps rule a problem out (SnNout). A very specific test, when positive, helps rule it in (SpPin). Likelihood ratios tell how much a result moves the odds.

concepts.ur: Sensitivity yeh hai ke masle wale logon mein test kitni baar positive aata hai. Specificity yeh hai ke masle ke baghair logon mein test kitni baar negative aata hai. Bohat sensitive test negative ho to masla rule out karne mein madad karta hai (SnNout). Bohat specific test positive ho to masla rule in karne mein madad karta hai (SpPin). Likelihood ratio batata hai ke result se chance kitna badla.

concepts.title: How to perform a test well
concepts.body: Most errors come from the set-up, not from the patient. Use the same position and the same force every time, and the same words.
bullets: Explain, ask permission and expose the joint.
Test the other side first so the patient learns what to expect and you learn their normal.
Stabilise the proximal segment and move only the segment you are testing.
Move slowly and stop when the patient says stop or when you feel a firm end-point.
Ask whether the pain is the patient's own pain, and where it is.
Tell the patient what you are going to do before you do it.
concepts.ur: Zyada tar ghaltiyan set-up se hoti hain, patient se nahi. Har baar wohi position, wohi force aur wohi alfaz istemal karein. Pehle samjhayein, ijazat lein aur joint ko expose karein. Pehle doosri side test karein taake patient ko pata chale aur aap ko unka normal maloom ho. Proximal hissa stabilise karein aur sirf test wala hissa hilayein. Aahista chalen aur jab patient roke ya firm end-point aaye to ruk jayein. Poochhein ke dard patient ka apna dard hai ya nahi.

concepts.title: Reading the result: what is positive?
concepts.body: A test can be positive in different ways. Always decide in advance which kind of positive you are looking for, because the same test can be positive by pain in one patient and by laxity in another.
concepts.ur: Test alag alag tareeqon se positive ho sakta hai. Pehle tay karein ke aap kis qism ka positive dhoond rahe hain, kyunke ek hi test kisi mein dard se aur kisi mein laxity se positive hota hai. Dard dobara paida hona, laxity ya zyada harkat, apprehension, kamzori ya lag, jhunjhunahat, aur clunk ya click ya locking — har ek ka matlab alag hai.

concepts.title: Clusters and decision rules
concepts.body: Several tests that agree are stronger than one test. Clusters and decision rules are made from combinations of findings that have been studied together.
bullets: Rotator cuff-related shoulder pain: a painful arc, pain or weakness on resisted external rotation and a positive Hawkins-Kennedy test.
Knee ligament: the Lachman test, the pivot shift test and the history of a twisting injury with swelling.
Wrist: Phalen, Tinel and the carpal compression test together with the symptom pattern.
Ottawa knee and ankle rules decide on imaging; they do not diagnose ligament injury.
concepts.ur: Kayi tests jo ek hi baat kahein, ek test se zyada mazboot hote hain. Clusters aur decision rules un findings ke mel se bante hain jinhein saath study kiya gaya. Rotator cuff dard ke liye painful arc, resisted external rotation par dard ya kamzori, aur Hawkins-Kennedy. Knee ligament ke liye Lachman, pivot shift aur twist injury ki history. Ottawa rules imaging ka faisla karte hain, ligament injury ki diagnosis nahi.

concepts.title: Timing, swelling and guarding
concepts.body: The same test gives different answers at different times. In the first hours a swollen, painful joint is guarded and hides laxity. After a few days the swelling settles and the test becomes more accurate.
bullets: Ankle ligaments: examine again four to five days after the injury.
Knee: a rapidly swollen knee suggests bleeding into the joint; do not push on a guarded knee.
Under anaesthesia the ACL tests are far more sensitive than in an awake patient.
Muscle guarding is a result in itself: note it.
concepts.ur: Ek hi test alag waqt par alag jawab deta hai. Pehle ghanton mein soojan aur dard wala joint guard karta hai aur laxity chhupa leta hai. Kuch din baad soojan kam hoti hai aur test zyada durust hota hai. Ankle ligaments ko injury ke chaar paanch din baad dobara examine karein. Tezi se soojha hua knee haemarthrosis ka ishara hai. Anaesthesia mein ACL tests zyada sensitive hote hain. Muscle guarding bhi ek result hai, use note karein.

concepts.title: When a test means refer
concepts.body: Some positive findings are not for rehabilitation alone. The test result changes the plan from treating to protecting and referring.
bullets: Suspected fracture after a fall (Ottawa rules, scaphoid tests): immobilise and image.
Suspected complete Achilles rupture: protect in plantarflexion and refer the same day.
Locked knee, or a knee that gives way with a new swelling: early orthopaedic opinion.
A large cuff tear signs (lag sign, drop arm) in an active patient: early specialist opinion.
A hot swollen joint with fever, or a swollen tender calf after surgery: urgent medical referral.
concepts.ur: Kuch positive findings sirf rehabilitation ke liye nahi hoti. Test ke result se plan treat karne se hifazat aur refer karne mein badal jata hai. Gir kar fracture ka shak (Ottawa rules, scaphoid tests): immobilise aur imaging. Achilles rupture ka shak: plantarflexion mein protect aur usi din refer. Locked knee: jaldi orthopaedic ray. Bari cuff tear ki alamat: jaldi specialist ray. Garam sooja joint bukhar ke saath, ya surgery ke baad sooji hui dardnak pindli: urgent doctor ko refer.

concepts.title: Recording and explaining the result
concepts.body: A clear record helps the next therapist and protects the patient. A clear explanation helps the patient understand.
bullets: Record side, test, the finding (pain, laxity, apprehension) and where it was felt.
Write the comparison with the other side and the end-point.
Say plainly what you found, what it suggests, and what you will do next.
Do not use a test name as a diagnosis; use it as evidence.
concepts.ur: Saaf record agle therapist ki madad karta hai aur patient ko mehfooz rakhta hai. Side, test, finding (dard, laxity, apprehension) aur jahan mehsoos hua, likhein. Doosri side se muqabla aur end-point likhein. Patient ko saaf alfaz mein batayein ke aap ne kya paya, iska kya matlab ho sakta hai aur agla qadam kya hoga. Test ka naam diagnosis na banayein, use saboot ki tarah istemal karein.

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Subacromial pain (rotator cuff-related shoulder pain)

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Standing or sitting, arms by the side; examiner in front or behind
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The patient raises the arm slowly through abduction in the scapular plane while the examiner watches the arc and asks where it hurts

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: Pain through the middle of the arc, roughly 60° to 120°, easing above and below it

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: A subacromial pain syndrome or rotator cuff-related shoulder pain; pain only at the very top of the arc points to the AC joint

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: Scapular dyskinesis, fear of movement or a stiff joint can change the arc; pain at the very top is not the same finding

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: Useful but not specific. It performs best in a small cluster (painful arc, pain or weakness on resisted external rotation, Hawkins-Kennedy) rather than alone.

atlas.title: Neer impingement test
atlas.subtitle: Pain from the subacromial space when the arm is raised to end range

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Pain from the subacromial space when the arm is raised to end range

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Sitting or standing; examiner beside the patient with one hand stopping the scapula from rotating
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: With the arm turned inwards, the examiner raises the arm passively in the scapular plane to the end of range while holding the scapula down

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: Pain in the front or side of the shoulder at the end of elevation

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: Pain from the rotator cuff or subacromial bursa (subacromial pain syndrome)

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: Any painful shoulder can hurt at the end of elevation, so the test is not specific; AC joint or biceps pain can mimic it

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: Good at including shoulders that hurt on elevation but poor at telling which structure is at fault. Interpret with the history, the painful arc and resisted tests.

atlas.title: Hawkins-Kennedy test
atlas.subtitle: Pain from the subacromial space during internal rotation

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Pain from the subacromial space during internal rotation

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Sitting or standing; arm raised to 90° with the elbow bent to 90°
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The examiner supports the arm and passively turns the shoulder into internal rotation by lowering the forearm

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: Pain in the shoulder during the movement

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: Subacromial pain syndrome or rotator cuff-related shoulder pain

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: Pain from the AC joint, biceps tendon or a stiff capsule gives the same answer; do not push into pain that is severe

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: Like Neer, it is sensitive but not specific, so a negative result makes a subacromial cause less likely while a positive one does not prove it.

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Supraspinatus strength and pain

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Standing or sitting; arms raised to 90° in the scapular plane, thumbs pointing down
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The patient holds the arm in that position while the examiner pushes down; the full can version has the thumbs pointing up

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: Pain or clear weakness against resistance

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: Supraspinatus tendinopathy or tear; pain without weakness points to tendon irritation

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: Pain can limit force and look like weakness; the empty can position loads the shoulder more painfully than the full can

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: The full can position tests the same weakness with less pain and is often preferred. Compare both sides and use it alongside the lag signs.

atlas.title: External rotation lag sign
atlas.subtitle: Full-thickness tear of supraspinatus or infraspinatus

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Full-thickness tear of supraspinatus or infraspinatus

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Sitting; elbow bent to 90° at the side
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The examiner takes the shoulder passively into almost full external rotation, supports the elbow and wrist, then lets go and asks the patient to hold the position

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: The forearm drifts back towards internal rotation (a lag)

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: A full-thickness tear of the posterior rotator cuff

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: A stiff shoulder cannot be placed in the start position; pain can make the patient give up and mimic a lag

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: Specific for large tears: a clear lag is strong evidence, but its absence does not rule a tear out. Pair it with the drop-arm and the Hornblower sign.

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Large rotator cuff tear (supraspinatus)

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Standing or sitting; examiner behind or beside the patient
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The examiner lifts the arm to 90° of abduction and asks the patient to lower it slowly to the side

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: The arm drops suddenly or the patient cannot lower it smoothly, usually with pain

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: A large, full-thickness supraspinatus tear

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: Pain can cause a sudden drop; a partial tear or tendinopathy usually passes the test

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: Poor sensitivity but good specificity: a positive test is meaningful, a negative one tells you little. Add the lag signs and strength testing.

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Teres minor (and infraspinatus) function

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Sitting; arm raised to 90° in the scapular plane, elbow bent to 90°
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The examiner supports the arm and asks the patient to rotate the forearm outwards against light resistance, as if lifting a horn to the mouth

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: The patient cannot hold the outward rotation and the forearm drops into internal rotation

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: A massive posterior rotator cuff tear involving teres minor

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: Pain or poor elevation range can stop the patient reaching the position

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: A positive test points to a large tear and needs referral; it is uncommon, so a negative result is common and uninformative.

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Subscapularis function

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Standing or sitting; hand flat on the belly with the elbow in front of the body
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The patient presses the hand into the belly while keeping the wrist straight and the elbow forward; the examiner may try to pull the hand away

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: The elbow drops backwards, the wrist flexes or the patient cannot press

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: A subscapularis tear or weakness

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: Pain, a tight chest or a weak patient can fail the test for other reasons; the elbow must stay in front

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: Easier on a painful shoulder than the lift-off test. A positive test is useful, but combine it with the lift-off and bear-hug tests.

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Subscapularis tear

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Standing or sitting; the back of the hand against the lower back
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The patient lifts the hand away from the back against the examiner's resistance

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: The patient cannot lift the hand off the back

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: A subscapularis tear

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: Needs enough internal rotation and extension to reach the start position, so it is often impossible when the shoulder is painful or stiff

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: Specific when positive, but frequently cannot be performed. Use the belly-press test when the start position hurts.

atlas.title: Speed's test
atlas.subtitle: Long head of biceps tendon pain, and labral pathology (SLAP)

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Long head of biceps tendon pain, and labral pathology (SLAP)

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Standing or sitting; arm forward to 90°, elbow straight, palm up
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The patient resists the examiner's downward pressure on the arm

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: Pain in the bicipital groove at the front of the shoulder

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: Biceps tendinopathy or a labral problem

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: Pain from the subacromial space during elevation can be mistaken for biceps pain

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: Only modestly accurate on its own; use it with Yergason's test and palpation of the groove.

atlas.title: Yergason's test
atlas.subtitle: Biceps tendon pain or instability in the bicipital groove

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Biceps tendon pain or instability in the bicipital groove

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Sitting; elbow bent to 90° and held against the side, forearm pronated
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The patient supinates the forearm and rotates the shoulder outwards against the examiner's resistance

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: Pain in the bicipital groove, or the tendon felt to click out of the groove

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: Biceps tendinopathy or a subluxing tendon

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: Resisted movement can provoke other shoulder structures; the groove must be palpated to confirm the source

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: Low accuracy as a single test. Combine it with Speed's test and tenderness over the groove.

atlas.title: O'Brien active compression test
atlas.subtitle: Labral (SLAP) tear and AC joint pain

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Labral (SLAP) tear and AC joint pain

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Standing; arm forward to 90°, a little across the body, thumb down
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The patient resists a downward force; the test is repeated with the palm facing up

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: Pain or a click deep inside the shoulder that is relieved with the palm up

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: A labral tear if the pain is deep inside the joint; the AC joint if the pain is on top of the shoulder

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: Accuracy for SLAP lesions is only fair and varies between studies; other painful shoulders can give a false positive

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: Weak on its own. Use a cluster of tests and imaging when the history strongly suggests a labral injury.

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Anterior glenohumeral instability

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Supine; shoulder abducted to 90° and the elbow bent to 90°
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The examiner slowly rotates the shoulder outwards; if apprehension appears, a backward force on the humeral head is applied and the apprehension should ease

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: A feeling that the shoulder will come out (apprehension), relieved by the relocating force

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: Anterior shoulder instability

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: Pain alone is not a positive test; the patient must show true apprehension. Stop before the shoulder is forced out

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: The apprehension itself, with relief on relocation, is the useful finding. Use the history of dislocation or subluxation first.

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Inferior glenohumeral laxity (multidirectional instability)

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Sitting or standing with the arm relaxed by the side
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The examiner pulls the arm downwards by the elbow or wrist and watches the space below the acromion

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: A visible gap (sulcus) appears below the acromion, graded by its depth; a sulcus that does not close in external rotation suggests rotator interval laxity

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: Inferior laxity, as in multidirectional instability or generalised hypermobility

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: Many healthy people with generalised laxity show a small sulcus; always compare with the other side

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: Use it as part of the picture with the history and other laxity tests; a positive sign without symptoms is not a diagnosis.

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Anterior and posterior glenohumeral laxity

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Sitting or lying; examiner holds the scapula and clavicle with one hand and the humeral head with the other
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The humeral head is pressed lightly into the socket (load) and then moved forwards and backwards (shift), and the amount of movement is graded

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: More translation than the other side, or the head rides to the rim of the socket or over it

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: Glenohumeral laxity in the direction tested

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: Muscle guarding hides laxity; laxity is not the same as instability

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: Laxity is common and often not painful, so link it to symptoms and to the apprehension test before calling it instability.

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Acromioclavicular (AC) joint pain

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Sitting or standing; arm raised to 90° forward
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The examiner moves the arm passively across the chest into horizontal adduction

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: Pain on top of the shoulder at the AC joint

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: AC joint arthritis or sprain

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: Pain at the back of the shoulder may be posterior capsule tightness, not the AC joint

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: Good for AC joint pain when the joint is also tender to palpation; a negative test helps to leave the AC joint out.

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Lateral epicondylalgia (tennis elbow)

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Sitting; elbow bent and supported, forearm turned palm down
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The patient makes a fist and extends the wrist against the examiner's resistance

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: Sharp pain over the lateral epicondyle

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: Tendinopathy of the common wrist extensor origin (lateral epicondylalgia)

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: Pain from the neck or the radial tunnel can reach the same area

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: A positive test with local tenderness is usually enough. If the pain does not behave like a tendon, look at the neck and the radial nerve.

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Lateral epicondylalgia (tennis elbow)

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Sitting; elbow straight, forearm turned palm down
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The examiner flexes the patient's wrist fully while the elbow stays straight, stretching the wrist extensors

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: Pain over the lateral epicondyle

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: Lateral epicondylalgia

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: Do not force the stretch into severe pain; a stiff wrist can give a false answer

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: Useful together with Cozen's test and palpation. A positive stretch and a positive resisted test support a tendon cause.

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Medial epicondylalgia (golfer's elbow)

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Sitting; elbow straight and forearm turned palm up
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The patient flexes the wrist against the examiner's resistance

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: Pain over the medial epicondyle

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: Tendinopathy of the common wrist flexor origin

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: Ulnar nerve irritation at the elbow can also cause medial pain and tingling

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: Check the ulnar nerve with Tinel's test and the elbow flexion test when there is tingling in the ring and little fingers.

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Medial (ulnar) collateral ligament laxity

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Sitting or supine; elbow bent to 20°-30° with the forearm turned palm up
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The examiner stabilises the upper arm and pushes the forearm outwards, opening the inner side of the joint

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: Pain or more opening than the other side, with a soft end-point

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: A sprain or tear of the medial collateral ligament, common in throwers

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: Testing with the elbow straight lets the bone lock the joint and hide laxity

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: Compare with the other side; a throwing history with medial pain makes the finding meaningful.

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Lateral collateral ligament laxity

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Sitting or supine; elbow bent to 20°-30°
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The examiner stabilises the upper arm and pushes the forearm inwards, opening the outer side of the joint

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: Pain or more opening than the other side, with a soft end-point

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: A lateral collateral ligament sprain or posterolateral instability after dislocation

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: Testing in full extension hides laxity; shoulder rotation changes the feel

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: Look at the history: a prior dislocation or fall on the outstretched hand makes the test far more meaningful.

atlas.title: Elbow flexion test
atlas.subtitle: Ulnar nerve compression at the cubital tunnel

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Ulnar nerve compression at the cubital tunnel

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Sitting; arms by the side
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The patient holds the elbow fully bent with the wrist extended for up to about one minute

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: Tingling or numbness in the ring and little finger within the minute

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: Cubital tunnel syndrome (ulnar nerve entrapment at the elbow)

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: Some healthy people have tingling with sustained elbow flexion; tap over the nerve as well (Tinel's) and compare both sides

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: Better when tingling appears early. Confirm with strength of the little finger and nerve conduction studies if symptoms persist.

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Carpal tunnel syndrome (median nerve)

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Sitting; elbows resting on a table
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The patient presses the backs of the hands together (wrists flexed) for up to 60 seconds

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: Tingling or numbness in the thumb, index and middle fingers

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: Median nerve compression in the carpal tunnel

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: Healthy people may feel mild tingling; stop at once if symptoms are strong

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: No single test settles carpal tunnel syndrome. Combine Phalen's, Tinel's, the carpal compression test and the symptom pattern.

atlas.title: Tinel's sign at the wrist
atlas.subtitle: Irritable median nerve at the carpal tunnel

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Irritable median nerve at the carpal tunnel

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Sitting; forearm supported with the palm up
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The examiner taps lightly over the median nerve at the front of the wrist

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: Tingling shooting into the thumb, index and middle fingers

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: Median nerve irritation in the carpal tunnel

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: A heavy tap causes tingling in anyone; tap lightly and compare with the other wrist

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: Moderate accuracy. It is more useful as part of a set of tests than alone.

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Carpal tunnel syndrome

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Sitting; forearm supported with the palm up
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The examiner presses firmly with both thumbs over the carpal tunnel for up to 30 seconds

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: Tingling or numbness in the median nerve distribution

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: Median nerve compression at the carpal tunnel

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: Pressing on the wrong place (over the tendons) or pressing very hard gives false results

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: Among the more useful single tests, and quicker than Phalen's. Best used with the history, the hand diagram and thumb muscle bulk.

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: De Quervain's tenosynovitis

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Sitting; forearm resting on the table with the hand in the neutral position
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The patient folds the thumb into the palm under the fingers; the wrist is then moved into ulnar deviation

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: Sharp pain over the radial side of the wrist at the first dorsal compartment

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: Inflammation of the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis tendons

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: Pain at the base of the thumb with grinding suggests thumb joint arthritis, not De Quervain's

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: A positive test with tenderness over the radial styloid is reliable enough to treat; the thumb grind test separates the two causes.

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Scapholunate ligament instability

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Sitting; the examiner holds the wrist with the thumb on the scaphoid tubercle
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: While pressing the scaphoid, the examiner moves the wrist from ulnar to radial deviation and releases the pressure

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: A painful clunk as the scaphoid slips over the rim of the radius

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: Scapholunate dissociation

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: Many healthy wrists have laxity and a click; look for pain and a difference from the other wrist

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: Relies on pain and comparison, not on a click alone. A positive test with a fall on the wrist needs imaging and hand-specialist advice.

atlas.title: Froment's sign
atlas.subtitle: Ulnar nerve weakness of the thumb adductor

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Ulnar nerve weakness of the thumb adductor

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Sitting; a flat piece of paper held between the thumb and the side of the index finger
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The examiner tries to pull the paper out while the patient grips it with straight thumbs

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: The thumb tip joint bends to keep hold of the paper

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: Weakness of adductor pollicis from an ulnar nerve lesion; flexor pollicis longus is compensating

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: Pain or a stiff thumb can produce the same posture; compare both hands

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: Pair it with sensation of the little finger and the small hand muscles to locate an ulnar nerve problem.

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Osteoarthritis of the thumb base

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Sitting; forearm supported
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The examiner presses the thumb metacarpal into the joint (axial load) and rotates it

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: Pain and sometimes grinding at the base of the thumb

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: Arthritis of the first carpometacarpal joint

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: Pain from De Quervain's tenosynovitis lies higher, over the radial styloid

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: A positive test with a bony base of the thumb, pain on pinch and an older patient is a strong picture.

atlas.title: Scaphoid fracture tests
atlas.subtitle: Possible scaphoid fracture after a fall on the hand

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Possible scaphoid fracture after a fall on the hand

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Sitting; wrist supported
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: Press the anatomical snuffbox, press the scaphoid tubercle at the base of the thumb on the palm side, and compress the thumb along its length

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: Pain at the snuffbox or tubercle, or pain on compression of the thumb

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: A possible scaphoid fracture, which may not show on the first X-ray

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: An early normal X-ray does not exclude a fracture; delay in diagnosis risks non-union and avascular necrosis

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: A cluster of three positive tests is very sensitive. Immobilise and arrange further imaging when the tests are positive, even if the first X-ray is normal.

atlas.title: FABER (Patrick) test
atlas.subtitle: Hip joint, sacroiliac joint and hip muscle pain

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Hip joint, sacroiliac joint and hip muscle pain

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Supine; the foot of the tested leg rests on the opposite knee
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The examiner presses the bent knee down towards the table while holding the opposite hip steady

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: Groin pain (hip joint), or pain over the back of the pelvis (sacroiliac joint), or a clearly smaller range than the other side

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: Hip joint pathology if the pain is in the groin; sacroiliac joint if the pain is behind

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: Pain location matters: the same test can be positive for the hip or the pelvis. Do not push into severe pain

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: Sensitive for hip pathology but not specific. Combine it with hip internal rotation range, FADIR and the history.

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Femoroacetabular impingement and labral irritation

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Supine
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The hip is bent to about 90°, then adducted and turned inwards (internal rotation) by the examiner

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: Pain in the groin that matches the patient's usual pain

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: An intra-articular hip problem such as femoroacetabular impingement or a labral tear

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: Pain from muscles, the pubic area or the lower back can mimic groin pain

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: High sensitivity and low specificity: a negative test makes impingement less likely, but a positive test alone does not prove it. Consider imaging only when surgery is considered.

atlas.title: Hip scour (quadrant) test
atlas.subtitle: Intra-articular hip pain and cartilage or labral damage

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Intra-articular hip pain and cartilage or labral damage

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Supine
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The hip is bent to 90° and the examiner presses along the thigh while moving the hip in an arc from adduction to abduction

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: Pain, catching or grinding in the groin or hip

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: An intra-articular hip problem such as arthritis or a labral tear

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: Compression through a very painful hip can be stopped early; do not force it

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: Adds weight to the picture with FABER and FADIR; it does not tell which structure is damaged.

atlas.title: Log roll test
atlas.subtitle: Pain from within the hip joint

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Pain from within the hip joint

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Supine with the legs straight and relaxed
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The examiner rolls the whole leg inwards and outwards by moving the thigh, keeping the muscles relaxed

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: Groin pain or a reduced or guarded rolling movement

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: An intra-articular hip problem (arthritis, fracture or infection in the right setting)

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: Muscle spasm can make rolling feel stiff; do not use it to exclude a fracture after a fall

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: Useful in a painful hip because it moves the joint with little muscle stretch; it is very sensitive for an intra-articular cause.

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Intra-articular hip pain under load

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Supine with the leg straight
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The patient lifts the leg to about 30° and holds it against the examiner's downward pressure

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: Groin pain

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: An intra-articular hip problem

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: Hip flexor or abdominal pain can be mistaken for hip pain; note where the pain is

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: One of several hip tests to combine; groin pain on loading and on rotation together is more persuasive.

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Hip abductor (gluteus medius) function

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Standing, barefoot, facing away from the examiner who watches the pelvis from behind
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The patient stands on one leg for about 30 seconds while the examiner watches the pelvis and trunk

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: The pelvis drops on the side of the lifted leg, or the trunk leans over the standing leg to compensate

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: Weakness or poor control of the gluteus medius of the standing leg

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: Pain, poor balance or a short leg can create a false drop; a trunk lean (compensated Trendelenburg) is also a positive sign

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: Reproducible and useful for planning gluteal strengthening; it does not tell the cause of the weakness (pain, nerve or muscle).

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) rupture

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Supine; knee bent to 20° to 30°, the examiner's one hand holds the thigh and the other the upper tibia
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The examiner pulls the tibia forward on the femur and judges the amount of movement and the feel of the end-point

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: More forward movement than the other side with a soft or missing end-point

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: A torn ACL

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: A knee bent too far, muscle guarding, a thigh too heavy to hold or a swollen painful knee all reduce accuracy

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: The best single clinical test for the ACL; it is more accurate than the anterior drawer, particularly when the knee is acutely swollen.

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: ACL rupture

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Supine; hip bent to 45° and knee to 90°, the examiner sits lightly on the foot
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: With the hamstrings relaxed, the examiner pulls the upper tibia forward and compares the movement with the other side

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: More forward movement than the other side, with a soft end-point

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: A torn ACL

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: Guarding from pain or swelling hides laxity; start with the posterior sag so a posterior tibial sag is not mistaken for forward movement

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: Less sensitive than the Lachman test in acute injuries; use both and decide from the whole picture.

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) rupture

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Supine; hip bent to 45° and knee to 90°, feet flat on the table
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: Look from the side for a sag of the upper tibia (sag sign), then push the tibia backwards with both thumbs on the joint line

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: The tibia sags backwards or moves further back than the other side with a soft end-point

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: A torn PCL

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: A sag that is not noticed can be mistaken for an anterior drawer, creating a false ACL finding

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: Accurate for a complete PCL tear. A positive test after a dashboard injury or a fall on a bent knee should lead to imaging.

atlas.title: Pivot shift test
atlas.subtitle: Rotatory instability from an ACL tear

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Rotatory instability from an ACL tear

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Supine; the examiner holds the foot and the outer knee
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: With the leg straight and turned inwards, a valgus force is applied while the knee is gradually bent

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: The tibia clunks or slips back into place at about 20° to 40° of flexion

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: A torn ACL with rotatory instability

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: An awake patient often guards, so a normal result does not exclude a tear

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: Very specific but not sensitive in the awake patient: a clear clunk is strong evidence, a negative test is not reassuring.

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Meniscal tear

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Supine; knee fully bent, the examiner holds the heel and the joint line
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The examiner turns the lower leg outwards with a valgus force (medial meniscus), or inwards with a varus force (lateral meniscus), then straightens the knee

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: A painful click or pain along the joint line

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: A tear of the meniscus on the side tested

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: Pain from arthritis or the patella can mimic it; some tears produce no click

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: Moderate accuracy. Combine it with joint line tenderness and the history (twist, locking, giving way) rather than relying on it alone.

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Meniscal tear under weight-bearing load

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Standing on the injured leg with the knee slightly bent (20°), holding the examiner's hands
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The patient twists the knee and body inwards and outwards three times while the knee stays bent

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: Joint line pain, catching or a feeling that the knee will lock

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: A meniscal tear

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: Reported accuracy was high in the first study and lower in later ones; weak or painful patients may not manage it

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: Reasonable as one of several tests; a positive result with locking in the history is meaningful.

atlas.title: Valgus stress test (knee)
atlas.subtitle: Medial collateral ligament (MCL) sprain or tear

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Medial collateral ligament (MCL) sprain or tear

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Supine; the knee is tested straight and again at 30° of flexion
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The examiner supports the leg and pushes the knee inwards (valgus) while pulling the ankle outwards

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: Pain, more opening of the inner joint line than the other side, or a soft end-point

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: An MCL injury; laxity at 30° alone suggests the MCL, laxity also when straight suggests the cruciate or capsule are involved

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: Rotation of the leg, or muscle guarding, changes the findings; the grade depends on the opening and the end-point

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: Grade by the opening and the end-point; a firm end-point suggests a partial tear. Laxity when straight needs investigation of other structures.

atlas.title: Varus stress test (knee)
atlas.subtitle: Lateral collateral ligament (LCL) and posterolateral corner injury

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Lateral collateral ligament (LCL) and posterolateral corner injury

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Supine; the knee is tested straight and again at 30° of flexion
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The examiner pushes the knee outwards (varus) while pulling the ankle inwards

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: Pain or more opening of the outer joint line than the other side

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: An LCL injury; laxity when straight suggests the posterolateral corner or cruciate ligaments are involved

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: Hip rotation and muscle guarding change the result; compare with the other leg

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: Injuries to the outer side of the knee are less common but easily missed; any laxity at 0° should lead to specialist assessment.

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Patellar instability

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Supine; knee relaxed and slightly bent (20° to 30°)
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The examiner pushes the patella gently outwards

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: The patient looks worried, tenses the thigh or stops the movement to avoid a dislocation

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: Patellar instability, typically after a previous dislocation

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: Pain alone is not a positive test; apprehension must be shown

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: Strengthens the history of a patella giving way; use the findings to plan strengthening and to decide when surgery is discussed.

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Fluid inside the knee joint

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Supine with the knee straight and the quadriceps relaxed
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: Sweep: stroke fluid up the inner side and then down the outer side and watch for a bulge. Patellar tap: squeeze fluid out of the pouch above the knee and tap the patella down

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: A bulge on the inner side after the sweep, or a tap felt as the patella floats and hits the femur

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: A knee effusion; swelling within a few hours of an injury suggests bleeding into the joint (haemarthrosis)

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: The sweep detects small amounts, the tap needs a larger effusion; a tight, overweight or very muscular knee is difficult to read

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: Rapid swelling after an injury is a warning: ligament tears, fractures and a locked knee need early assessment.

atlas.title: Ottawa knee rule
atlas.subtitle: Deciding whether an X-ray is needed after an acute knee injury

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Deciding whether an X-ray is needed after an acute knee injury

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Any position; examine and ask the patient to walk
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: Check the five items: age 55 or more, tenderness of the head of the fibula, isolated tenderness of the patella, inability to bend the knee to 90°, and inability to take four steps both at the time of injury and now

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: Any one of the five items

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: An X-ray is needed to look for a fracture

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: The rule is for acute injuries and was developed for adults; it does not exclude ligament or meniscus injury

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: Very sensitive for fractures: if none of the five items is present, a fracture is unlikely. It is a decision rule, not a diagnosis.

atlas.title: Anterior drawer test (ankle)
atlas.subtitle: Anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL) sprain or tear

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL) sprain or tear

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Sitting with the knee bent or supine; ankle relaxed in about 10° to 20° of plantarflexion
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The examiner holds the lower leg still and pulls the heel forward, comparing the movement and the end-point with the other ankle

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: More forward movement than the other side, a soft end-point or a dimple in front of the lateral malleolus (suction sign)

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: An ATFL sprain or rupture

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: Swelling and pain in the first days hide laxity; ankle too far plantarflexed or the leg not held still

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: More accurate when repeated four to five days after the injury, once swelling and guarding have settled.

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Calcaneofibular ligament (CFL) and ATFL laxity

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Sitting or supine; ankle in neutral
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The examiner holds the lower leg and tilts the heel inwards (inversion), comparing the tilt with the other ankle

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: More tilt than the other side or pain over the lateral ligaments

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: A CFL sprain or tear, often with the ATFL

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: Pain guarding, and normal differences between ankles, can change the result

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: Use together with the anterior drawer and palpation; a severe tilt suggests both ligaments are injured.

atlas.title: Squeeze test (syndesmosis)
atlas.subtitle: Injury of the syndesmosis (high ankle sprain)

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Injury of the syndesmosis (high ankle sprain)

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Sitting or supine; leg relaxed
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The examiner squeezes the tibia and fibula together at the middle of the calf, and watches for pain at the ankle

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: Pain at the front of the ankle between the tibia and fibula, far from the squeeze

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: A syndesmosis injury

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: Pain at the squeeze site is not a positive result; the pain must appear at the ankle

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: High ankle sprains heal more slowly and can need protection. Repeat the test with the external rotation test, and consider imaging when weight-bearing is painful.

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Syndesmosis and deltoid ligament injury

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Sitting with the knee bent to 90°; ankle in neutral
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The examiner holds the leg still and turns the foot outwards

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: Pain at the syndesmosis in front of the ankle, or at the inner side of the ankle

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: A syndesmosis sprain or a deltoid ligament sprain

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: Too much force can aggravate a painful ankle; compare with the other side

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: One of the more useful tests for a high ankle sprain; use it together with the squeeze test.

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Achilles tendon rupture

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Lying face down with the feet over the end of the bed, or kneeling on a chair
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The examiner squeezes the calf and watches the foot

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: The foot does not point down (no plantarflexion) when the calf is squeezed

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: A complete rupture of the Achilles tendon

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: Other plantarflexors can move the foot a little; a partial tear can give a normal result

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: Reliable when positive. Add a palpable gap, weakness of calf raising, and the Matles test (the foot rests in less plantarflexion when the knee is bent to 90°). Refer the same day.

atlas.title: Windlass test
atlas.subtitle: Plantar heel pain from the plantar fascia

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Plantar heel pain from the plantar fascia

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Standing or with the foot hanging over the edge of the bed
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The examiner extends the big toe at the first joint, tightening the plantar fascia

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: The patient's heel or arch pain is reproduced

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: Plantar fasciopathy (plantar heel pain)

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: Pain from the big toe joint itself can be confused with heel pain; note where it hurts

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: Supports a plantar fascia cause when combined with pain on the first steps in the morning and tenderness at the heel.

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Morton's neuroma and metatarsalgia

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Sitting or supine; the foot is held in the examiner's hand
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: The examiner squeezes the metatarsal heads together while pressing the web space between the toes

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: Pain or a click between the toes, with tingling or burning into the toes

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: An interdigital (Morton's) neuroma

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: Joint pain between the metatarsals can look similar; a click alone is not enough

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: Useful with the history of burning pain in narrow shoes. Imaging is only needed if treatment fails.

atlas.title: Ottawa ankle rules
atlas.subtitle: Deciding whether an X-ray is needed after an ankle or midfoot injury

fields.label: Purpose
fields.value: Deciding whether an X-ray is needed after an ankle or midfoot injury

fields.label: Position
fields.value: Examine the bones and ask the patient to walk four steps
fields.ask: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the {title}?

fields.label: Method
fields.value: Ankle X-ray if there is pain near the ankle and bone tenderness at the back edge or tip of either malleolus, or inability to take four steps. Foot X-ray if there is midfoot pain with tenderness at the base of the fifth metatarsal or the navicular, or inability to take four steps

fields.label: Positive finding
fields.value: Any of those findings

fields.label: What a positive suggests
fields.value: An X-ray is needed to look for a fracture

fields.label: Pitfalls
fields.value: The rules were made for adults with acute injuries and do not rule out ligament injury

fields.label: How far to trust it
fields.value: Highly sensitive: a negative result makes a fracture very unlikely and avoids unnecessary X-rays.

questions.prompt: A very sensitive test is negative. What is it best at?
options: Ruling the problem out
Grading the problem
Treating the problem
Ruling the problem in
questions.explain: A highly sensitive test misses few people with the problem, so a negative result helps to rule it out (SnNout).

questions.prompt: Which is the best single clinical test for an ACL rupture?
options: Patellar tap
Lachman test
McMurray test
Valgus stress test
questions.explain: The Lachman test is the most accurate single clinical test for the ACL.

questions.prompt: Phalen's test is used to assess which problem?
options: Scaphoid fracture
Tennis elbow
Carpal tunnel syndrome
De Quervain's tenosynovitis
questions.explain: Sustained wrist flexion tests for median nerve compression in the carpal tunnel.

questions.prompt: What is a positive Thompson test?
options: Pain on squeezing the calf
Weak toe raising
Swelling of the calf
No plantarflexion when the calf is squeezed
questions.explain: No movement of the foot on a calf squeeze suggests a complete Achilles rupture.

questions.prompt: Finkelstein's test looks for which condition?
options: Cubital tunnel syndrome
Scapholunate instability
De Quervain's tenosynovitis
Carpal tunnel syndrome
questions.explain: Ulnar deviation with the thumb in the palm stretches the first dorsal compartment tendons.

questions.prompt: Which movements make up the FADIR position?
options: Flexion, abduction and external rotation
Flexion, adduction and internal rotation
Flexion, abduction and internal rotation
Extension, adduction and internal rotation
questions.explain: FADIR stands for flexion, adduction and internal rotation.

questions.prompt: In a positive Trendelenburg test the pelvis drops on which side?
options: Neither side
The side of the standing leg
The side of the lifted leg
Both sides equally
questions.explain: The pelvis falls on the lifted side because the gluteus medius of the standing leg cannot hold it level.

questions.prompt: Cozen's test is a resisted movement of which kind?
options: Wrist flexion
Forearm supination only
Elbow flexion
Wrist extension
questions.explain: Resisted wrist extension loads the extensor origin at the lateral epicondyle.

questions.prompt: The sulcus sign points to which problem?
options: AC joint arthritis
Biceps rupture
Inferior shoulder laxity
Rotator cuff tear
questions.explain: A gap below the acromion on downward traction shows inferior glenohumeral laxity.

questions.prompt: What are the Ottawa ankle rules for?
options: Deciding if an X-ray is needed
Measuring laxity
Choosing a brace
Grading a sprain
questions.explain: They help decide whether an ankle or foot X-ray is needed after an acute injury.

questions.prompt: What is a positive apprehension test?
options: The patient has any pain
The joint is stiff
The joint clicks
The patient fears the joint will come out
questions.explain: Fear of dislocation, not only pain, is the positive finding.

questions.prompt: Why compare a test with the other side?
options: Normal laxity differs between people
It saves time
The other side is always normal
It reduces pain
questions.explain: Each person has their own normal range; the other side is the best reference.

questions.prompt: At what knee angle is the Lachman test done?
options: 90° of flexion
120° of flexion
Full extension
20° to 30° of flexion
questions.explain: A small amount of flexion relaxes the hamstrings and lets the ACL be tested cleanly.

questions.prompt: A positive drop-arm test suggests tear of which tendon?
options: Long head of biceps
Subscapularis
Supraspinatus
Pectoralis major
questions.explain: A patient who cannot lower the abducted arm smoothly may have a large supraspinatus tear.

questions.prompt: Valgus laxity at 30° of knee flexion but not at 0° suggests what?
options: A PCL injury
An isolated MCL injury
An ACL tear only
A meniscal tear
questions.explain: At 30° the cruciates are relaxed, so laxity then points to the MCL.

questions.prompt: Which McMurray manoeuvre tests the lateral meniscus?
options: Internal rotation with a varus force
Flexion with distraction
Extension with compression only
External rotation with a valgus force
questions.explain: The lower leg is turned inwards with a varus force to stress the lateral meniscus.

questions.prompt: A positive belly-press test suggests weakness of which muscle?
options: Supraspinatus
Teres minor
Infraspinatus
Subscapularis
questions.explain: A dropped elbow or flexed wrist on pressing shows subscapularis weakness.

questions.prompt: Which ligament does the ankle anterior drawer test mainly assess?
options: Anterior talofibular ligament
Deltoid ligament
Plantar fascia
Spring ligament
questions.explain: A forward pull of the heel stresses the ATFL.

questions.prompt: Where must the pain appear in the squeeze test to be positive?
options: At the site of the squeeze
In the big toe
At the ankle, far from the squeeze
In the heel
questions.explain: Pain between the tibia and fibula at the ankle suggests a syndesmosis injury.

questions.prompt: What is the position for Speed's test?
options: Arm forward to 90°, elbow straight, palm up
Arm above the head
Arm behind the back
Arm at the side, elbow bent, palm down
questions.explain: Resisted forward elevation with the palm up loads the long head of biceps.

questions.prompt: The sweep test detects what?
options: A torn meniscus
A ligament tear
Patellar maltracking
A small knee effusion
questions.explain: A bulge on the inner side after a sweep shows a small amount of fluid.

questions.prompt: Why is a negative pivot shift test in an awake patient not reassuring?
options: The test is not specific
It is painful
It only tests the PCL
Guarding hides the finding, so sensitivity is low
questions.explain: A clunk is strong evidence for a tear, but a negative result does not exclude it.

questions.prompt: A negative FADIR makes which problem less likely?
options: Femoroacetabular impingement
Hip osteoarthritis only
Lumbar stenosis
A hamstring tear
questions.explain: FADIR is sensitive for intra-articular hip pain, so a negative test makes impingement less likely.

questions.prompt: Pain only at the very top of the painful arc suggests which structure?
options: The subscapularis
The AC joint
The glenoid labrum
The biceps long head
questions.explain: Pain near the end of elevation is classically an AC joint sign.

questions.prompt: When is the ankle anterior drawer test most accurate?
options: Four to five days after the injury
Under no circumstances
Only after surgery
Immediately after the injury
questions.explain: Swelling and guarding settle in the first few days, so a delayed exam is more accurate.

questions.prompt: What does a negative McMurray test tell you?
options: The meniscus is normal
The ACL is intact
The joint is stable
It does not exclude a meniscal tear
questions.explain: McMurray has only moderate sensitivity, so a negative test is not enough.

questions.prompt: Why does a syndesmosis sprain need special attention?
options: It often heals more slowly than a lateral sprain
It never needs rest
It is always a fracture
It heals faster
questions.explain: High ankle sprains take longer to settle and may need protection.

questions.prompt: A posterior sag of the tibia at 90° of knee flexion suggests what?
options: An ACL tear
A meniscal tear
A PCL tear
An MCL tear
questions.explain: The tibia sags backwards when the PCL is torn.

questions.prompt: In O'Brien's test, pain relieved with the palm up suggests what?
options: A labral problem
A rotator cuff tear
Biceps rupture
AC joint arthritis
questions.explain: Deep pain that eases with the palm up points to the labrum, while top-of-shoulder pain points to the AC joint.

questions.prompt: Why combine several tests?
options: To use more time
To make the patient tired
Each test is always accurate
Agreement between tests is stronger than one test
questions.explain: A cluster of tests that agree is more persuasive than any single test.

questions.prompt: What do you do next?
options: Push harder on the Lachman test
Ignore the swelling and test for the pivot shift
Declare the ACL intact and start strengthening
Retest in a few days when the swelling settles, and refer for imaging
questions.explain: A guarded swollen knee hides laxity. Reassess after the swelling settles and image the knee.
questions.case: A 24-year-old footballer twisted the knee two hours ago. The knee is swollen, painful and guarded. Lachman cannot be done.

questions.prompt: What is the right management?
options: Treat as a fracture: immobilise and repeat or advance the imaging
Apply a stretching programme
Reassure and start strengthening
Treat as De Quervain's tenosynovitis
questions.explain: Snuffbox tenderness after a fall on the hand needs immobilisation until a scaphoid fracture is excluded.
questions.case: A 30-year-old fell on an outstretched hand. The first wrist X-ray is normal, but the anatomical snuffbox is tender and thumb compression hurts.

questions.prompt: What should you do first?
options: Reassure the patient
Arrange an ankle X-ray
Start a strengthening programme
Do a talar tilt only
questions.explain: Bone tenderness at the back edge of the malleolus or inability to take four steps means an ankle X-ray under the Ottawa rules.
questions.case: After inverting an ankle the patient cannot take four steps and has bone tenderness at the back edge of the lateral malleolus.

questions.prompt: What is the appropriate action?
options: Massage the calf
Advise rest for a week and review
Protect the leg and refer the same day
Start calf stretching
questions.explain: A positive Thompson test with a gap suggests a complete Achilles rupture and needs urgent referral.
questions.case: While sprinting a patient felt a sudden pop in the calf. The Thompson test is positive and a gap can be felt in the tendon.

questions.prompt: What does this suggest and what is the next step?
options: Simple subacromial pain; start exercises only
A frozen shoulder; start stretching
A normal shoulder
A large full-thickness cuff tear; refer for imaging and specialist opinion
questions.explain: A lag sign and a positive drop-arm test in a person with weakness suggest a large tear that needs imaging and an orthopaedic opinion.
questions.case: A 58-year-old has night pain, cannot hold the arm in external rotation (lag sign) and has a positive drop-arm test.

questions.prompt: Which diagnosis is most likely?
options: Anterior shoulder instability
AC joint arthritis
Rotator cuff tendinopathy
Frozen shoulder
questions.explain: Apprehension relieved by a relocating force in a young athlete is typical of anterior instability.
questions.case: A 22-year-old rugby player feels the shoulder will come out when it is abducted and turned outwards. A backward force on the humeral head relieves the feeling.

questions.prompt: What is the best next step?
options: Reassure and advise rest only
Refer for nerve conduction studies and a specialist opinion
Test again next year
Give stretching exercises only
questions.explain: Thenar wasting means advanced median nerve compression and needs prompt specialist assessment.
questions.case: A patient has night numbness in the hand, a positive Phalen test and a positive Tinel's sign, with wasting of the thumb muscle.

questions.prompt: What should you suspect and do?
options: A grade III MCL tear with possible cruciate injury; refer for assessment
A normal knee
A patellar problem
A meniscal tear only; start strengthening
questions.explain: Valgus laxity when straight and at 30° with no firm end-point suggests the cruciate ligaments or capsule are also injured.
questions.case: After a ski fall the knee opens on valgus stress both straight and at 30° with no firm end-point.

questions.prompt: Which interpretation is best?
options: A hamstring strain
A normal hip
Definite labral tear that needs surgery now
Possible femoroacetabular impingement; assess hip rotation and decide on imaging only if surgery is considered
questions.explain: Positive tests suggest an intra-articular hip problem but they are not specific; imaging is for those considering surgery.
questions.case: A 25-year-old athlete has groin pain with a positive FADIR and a positive FABER test.

questions.prompt: What should you also examine?
options: Only the elbow
Nothing else
The neck, because the pain may come from the cervical spine
Only the wrist
questions.explain: If arm pain is provoked by neck movement, check the cervical spine and nerve roots even when Cozen's test is positive.
questions.case: A patient has lateral elbow pain with a positive Cozen's test, but turning the neck also reproduces the arm pain.

questions.prompt: What does the Painful arc look for?
options: Biceps tendon pain or instability in the bicipital groove
Pain from the subacromial space when the arm is raised to end range
Subacromial pain (rotator cuff-related shoulder pain)
Supraspinatus strength and pain
questions.explain: Painful arc: purpose — Subacromial pain (rotator cuff-related shoulder pain).

questions.prompt: How is the Painful arc performed?
options: The examiner supports the arm and passively turns the shoulder into internal rotation by lowering the forearm
The patient raises the arm slowly through abduction in the scapular plane while the examiner watches the arc and asks where it hurts
The examiner takes the shoulder passively into almost full external rotation, supports the elbow and wrist, then lets go and asks the patient to hold the position
The examiner supports the arm and asks the patient to rotate the forearm outwards against light resistance, as if lifting a horn to the mouth
questions.explain: Painful arc: method — The patient raises the arm slowly through abduction in the scapular plane while the examiner watches the arc and asks where it hurts.

questions.prompt: What is a positive Painful arc?
options: The forearm drifts back towards internal rotation (a lag)
Pain or clear weakness against resistance
Pain in the bicipital groove, or the tendon felt to click out of the groove
Pain through the middle of the arc, roughly 60° to 120°, easing above and below it
questions.explain: Painful arc: positive finding — Pain through the middle of the arc, roughly 60° to 120°, easing above and below it.

questions.prompt: What does a positive Painful arc suggest?
options: A subacromial pain syndrome or rotator cuff-related shoulder pain; pain only at the very top of the arc points to the AC joint
Pain from the rotator cuff or subacromial bursa (subacromial pain syndrome)
A large, full-thickness supraspinatus tear
A subscapularis tear
questions.explain: Painful arc: what a positive suggests — A subacromial pain syndrome or rotator cuff-related shoulder pain; pain only at the very top of the arc points to the AC joint.

questions.prompt: What does the Neer impingement test look for?
options: Pain from the subacromial space when the arm is raised to end range
Labral (SLAP) tear and AC joint pain
Large rotator cuff tear (supraspinatus)
Pain from the subacromial space during internal rotation
questions.explain: Neer impingement test: purpose — Pain from the subacromial space when the arm is raised to end range.

questions.prompt: How is the Neer impingement test performed?
options: The patient resists a downward force; the test is repeated with the palm facing up
With the arm turned inwards, the examiner raises the arm passively in the scapular plane to the end of range while holding the scapula down
The patient lifts the hand away from the back against the examiner's resistance
The examiner supports the arm and asks the patient to rotate the forearm outwards against light resistance, as if lifting a horn to the mouth
questions.explain: Neer impingement test: method — With the arm turned inwards, the examiner raises the arm passively in the scapular plane to the end of range while holding the scapula down.

questions.prompt: What is a positive Neer impingement test?
options: The patient cannot hold the outward rotation and the forearm drops into internal rotation
The forearm drifts back towards internal rotation (a lag)
Pain in the bicipital groove at the front of the shoulder
Pain in the front or side of the shoulder at the end of elevation
questions.explain: Neer impingement test: positive finding — Pain in the front or side of the shoulder at the end of elevation.

questions.prompt: What does a positive Neer impingement test suggest?
options: Anterior shoulder instability
A subacromial pain syndrome or rotator cuff-related shoulder pain; pain only at the very top of the arc points to the AC joint
Pain from the rotator cuff or subacromial bursa (subacromial pain syndrome)
A labral tear if the pain is deep inside the joint; the AC joint if the pain is on top of the shoulder
questions.explain: Neer impingement test: what a positive suggests — Pain from the rotator cuff or subacromial bursa (subacromial pain syndrome).

questions.prompt: What does the Hawkins-Kennedy test look for?
options: Teres minor (and infraspinatus) function
Subscapularis function
Pain from the subacromial space during internal rotation
Supraspinatus strength and pain
questions.explain: Hawkins-Kennedy test: purpose — Pain from the subacromial space during internal rotation.

questions.prompt: How is the Hawkins-Kennedy test performed?
options: The examiner takes the shoulder passively into almost full external rotation, supports the elbow and wrist, then lets go and asks the patient to hold the position
With the arm turned inwards, the examiner raises the arm passively in the scapular plane to the end of range while holding the scapula down
The examiner supports the arm and passively turns the shoulder into internal rotation by lowering the forearm
The examiner lifts the arm to 90° of abduction and asks the patient to lower it slowly to the side
questions.explain: Hawkins-Kennedy test: method — The examiner supports the arm and passively turns the shoulder into internal rotation by lowering the forearm.

questions.prompt: What is a positive Hawkins-Kennedy test?
options: Pain or clear weakness against resistance
Pain in the front or side of the shoulder at the end of elevation
The elbow drops backwards, the wrist flexes or the patient cannot press
Pain in the shoulder during the movement
