questions.explain: Hawkins-Kennedy test: positive finding — Pain in the shoulder during the movement.

questions.prompt: What does a positive Hawkins-Kennedy test suggest?
options: A large, full-thickness supraspinatus tear
A subscapularis tear
Subacromial pain syndrome or rotator cuff-related shoulder pain
A massive posterior rotator cuff tear involving teres minor
questions.explain: Hawkins-Kennedy test: what a positive suggests — Subacromial pain syndrome or rotator cuff-related shoulder pain.

questions.prompt: What does the Empty can (Jobe) test look for?
options: Supraspinatus strength and pain
Biceps tendon pain or instability in the bicipital groove
Large rotator cuff tear (supraspinatus)
Pain from the subacromial space during internal rotation
questions.explain: Empty can (Jobe) test: purpose — Supraspinatus strength and pain.

questions.prompt: How is the Empty can (Jobe) test performed?
options: The examiner lifts the arm to 90° of abduction and asks the patient to lower it slowly to the side
The patient holds the arm in that position while the examiner pushes down; the full can version has the thumbs pointing up
The examiner takes the shoulder passively into almost full external rotation, supports the elbow and wrist, then lets go and asks the patient to hold the position
The patient resists the examiner's downward pressure on the arm
questions.explain: Empty can (Jobe) test: method — The patient holds the arm in that position while the examiner pushes down; the full can version has the thumbs pointing up.

questions.prompt: What is a positive Empty can (Jobe) test?
options: Pain in the front or side of the shoulder at the end of elevation
The patient cannot hold the outward rotation and the forearm drops into internal rotation
The forearm drifts back towards internal rotation (a lag)
Pain or clear weakness against resistance
questions.explain: Empty can (Jobe) test: positive finding — Pain or clear weakness against resistance.

questions.prompt: What does a positive Empty can (Jobe) test suggest?
options: Supraspinatus tendinopathy or tear; pain without weakness points to tendon irritation
Subacromial pain syndrome or rotator cuff-related shoulder pain
A full-thickness tear of the posterior rotator cuff
A subacromial pain syndrome or rotator cuff-related shoulder pain; pain only at the very top of the arc points to the AC joint
questions.explain: Empty can (Jobe) test: what a positive suggests — Supraspinatus tendinopathy or tear; pain without weakness points to tendon irritation.

questions.prompt: What does the External rotation lag sign look for?
options: Full-thickness tear of supraspinatus or infraspinatus
Subacromial pain (rotator cuff-related shoulder pain)
Biceps tendon pain or instability in the bicipital groove
Pain from the subacromial space during internal rotation
questions.explain: External rotation lag sign: purpose — Full-thickness tear of supraspinatus or infraspinatus.

questions.prompt: How is the External rotation lag sign performed?
options: The examiner supports the arm and passively turns the shoulder into internal rotation by lowering the forearm
With the arm turned inwards, the examiner raises the arm passively in the scapular plane to the end of range while holding the scapula down
The patient holds the arm in that position while the examiner pushes down; the full can version has the thumbs pointing up
The examiner takes the shoulder passively into almost full external rotation, supports the elbow and wrist, then lets go and asks the patient to hold the position
questions.explain: External rotation lag sign: method — The examiner takes the shoulder passively into almost full external rotation, supports the elbow and wrist, then lets go and asks the patient to hold the position.

questions.prompt: What is a positive External rotation lag sign?
options: Pain in the bicipital groove at the front of the shoulder
The forearm drifts back towards internal rotation (a lag)
The patient cannot lift the hand off the back
Pain in the bicipital groove, or the tendon felt to click out of the groove
questions.explain: External rotation lag sign: positive finding — The forearm drifts back towards internal rotation (a lag).

questions.prompt: What does a positive External rotation lag sign suggest?
options: A full-thickness tear of the posterior rotator cuff
Subacromial pain syndrome or rotator cuff-related shoulder pain
A large, full-thickness supraspinatus tear
A subscapularis tear or weakness
questions.explain: External rotation lag sign: what a positive suggests — A full-thickness tear of the posterior rotator cuff.

questions.prompt: What does the Drop-arm test look for?
options: Large rotator cuff tear (supraspinatus)
Full-thickness tear of supraspinatus or infraspinatus
Long head of biceps tendon pain, and labral pathology (SLAP)
Labral (SLAP) tear and AC joint pain
questions.explain: Drop-arm test: purpose — Large rotator cuff tear (supraspinatus).

questions.prompt: How is the Drop-arm test performed?
options: The patient raises the arm slowly through abduction in the scapular plane while the examiner watches the arc and asks where it hurts
The examiner lifts the arm to 90° of abduction and asks the patient to lower it slowly to the side
With the arm turned inwards, the examiner raises the arm passively in the scapular plane to the end of range while holding the scapula down
The examiner supports the arm and asks the patient to rotate the forearm outwards against light resistance, as if lifting a horn to the mouth
questions.explain: Drop-arm test: method — The examiner lifts the arm to 90° of abduction and asks the patient to lower it slowly to the side.

questions.prompt: What is a positive Drop-arm test?
options: Pain in the front or side of the shoulder at the end of elevation
Pain or clear weakness against resistance
The patient cannot hold the outward rotation and the forearm drops into internal rotation
The arm drops suddenly or the patient cannot lower it smoothly, usually with pain
questions.explain: Drop-arm test: positive finding — The arm drops suddenly or the patient cannot lower it smoothly, usually with pain.

questions.prompt: What does a positive Drop-arm test suggest?
options: A large, full-thickness supraspinatus tear
A subscapularis tear or weakness
A subacromial pain syndrome or rotator cuff-related shoulder pain; pain only at the very top of the arc points to the AC joint
A full-thickness tear of the posterior rotator cuff
questions.explain: Drop-arm test: what a positive suggests — A large, full-thickness supraspinatus tear.

questions.prompt: What does the Hornblower's sign look for?
options: Pain from the subacromial space when the arm is raised to end range
Subscapularis function
Teres minor (and infraspinatus) function
Subacromial pain (rotator cuff-related shoulder pain)
questions.explain: Hornblower's sign: purpose — Teres minor (and infraspinatus) function.

questions.prompt: How is the Hornblower's sign performed?
options: The patient resists a downward force; the test is repeated with the palm facing up
The examiner supports the arm and asks the patient to rotate the forearm outwards against light resistance, as if lifting a horn to the mouth
The patient supinates the forearm and rotates the shoulder outwards against the examiner's resistance
The examiner lifts the arm to 90° of abduction and asks the patient to lower it slowly to the side
questions.explain: Hornblower's sign: method — The examiner supports the arm and asks the patient to rotate the forearm outwards against light resistance, as if lifting a horn to the mouth.

questions.prompt: What is a positive Hornblower's sign?
options: Pain in the shoulder during the movement
Pain or clear weakness against resistance
Pain in the bicipital groove at the front of the shoulder
The patient cannot hold the outward rotation and the forearm drops into internal rotation
questions.explain: Hornblower's sign: positive finding — The patient cannot hold the outward rotation and the forearm drops into internal rotation.

questions.prompt: What does a positive Hornblower's sign suggest?
options: A massive posterior rotator cuff tear involving teres minor
A labral tear if the pain is deep inside the joint; the AC joint if the pain is on top of the shoulder
Supraspinatus tendinopathy or tear; pain without weakness points to tendon irritation
Subacromial pain syndrome or rotator cuff-related shoulder pain
questions.explain: Hornblower's sign: what a positive suggests — A massive posterior rotator cuff tear involving teres minor.

questions.prompt: What does the Belly-press test look for?
options: Pain from the subacromial space during internal rotation
Full-thickness tear of supraspinatus or infraspinatus
Subscapularis function
Pain from the subacromial space when the arm is raised to end range
questions.explain: Belly-press test: purpose — Subscapularis function.

questions.prompt: How is the Belly-press test performed?
options: With the arm turned inwards, the examiner raises the arm passively in the scapular plane to the end of range while holding the scapula down
The patient presses the hand into the belly while keeping the wrist straight and the elbow forward; the examiner may try to pull the hand away
The examiner supports the arm and asks the patient to rotate the forearm outwards against light resistance, as if lifting a horn to the mouth
The patient resists a downward force; the test is repeated with the palm facing up
questions.explain: Belly-press test: method — The patient presses the hand into the belly while keeping the wrist straight and the elbow forward; the examiner may try to pull the hand away.

questions.prompt: What is a positive Belly-press test?
options: Pain in the bicipital groove, or the tendon felt to click out of the groove
The patient cannot hold the outward rotation and the forearm drops into internal rotation
The patient cannot lift the hand off the back
The elbow drops backwards, the wrist flexes or the patient cannot press
questions.explain: Belly-press test: positive finding — The elbow drops backwards, the wrist flexes or the patient cannot press.

questions.prompt: What does a positive Belly-press test suggest?
options: A subscapularis tear or weakness
A massive posterior rotator cuff tear involving teres minor
A subacromial pain syndrome or rotator cuff-related shoulder pain; pain only at the very top of the arc points to the AC joint
Subacromial pain syndrome or rotator cuff-related shoulder pain
questions.explain: Belly-press test: what a positive suggests — A subscapularis tear or weakness.

questions.prompt: What does the Lift-off test (Gerber) look for?
options: Pain from the subacromial space when the arm is raised to end range
Subscapularis tear
Biceps tendon pain or instability in the bicipital groove
Long head of biceps tendon pain, and labral pathology (SLAP)
questions.explain: Lift-off test (Gerber): purpose — Subscapularis tear.

questions.prompt: How is the Lift-off test (Gerber) performed?
options: The examiner supports the arm and passively turns the shoulder into internal rotation by lowering the forearm
The patient resists the examiner's downward pressure on the arm
The patient lifts the hand away from the back against the examiner's resistance
The patient raises the arm slowly through abduction in the scapular plane while the examiner watches the arc and asks where it hurts
questions.explain: Lift-off test (Gerber): method — The patient lifts the hand away from the back against the examiner's resistance.

questions.prompt: What is a positive Lift-off test (Gerber)?
options: The patient cannot lift the hand off the back
Pain through the middle of the arc, roughly 60° to 120°, easing above and below it
The forearm drifts back towards internal rotation (a lag)
Pain in the front or side of the shoulder at the end of elevation
questions.explain: Lift-off test (Gerber): positive finding — The patient cannot lift the hand off the back.

questions.prompt: What does a positive Lift-off test (Gerber) suggest?
options: Inferior laxity, as in multidirectional instability or generalised hypermobility
A large, full-thickness supraspinatus tear
A subscapularis tear
Supraspinatus tendinopathy or tear; pain without weakness points to tendon irritation
questions.explain: Lift-off test (Gerber): what a positive suggests — A subscapularis tear.

questions.prompt: What does the Speed's test look for?
options: Long head of biceps tendon pain, and labral pathology (SLAP)
Subscapularis function
Pain from the subacromial space during internal rotation
Teres minor (and infraspinatus) function
questions.explain: Speed's test: purpose — Long head of biceps tendon pain, and labral pathology (SLAP).

questions.prompt: How is the Speed's test performed?
options: With the arm turned inwards, the examiner raises the arm passively in the scapular plane to the end of range while holding the scapula down
The examiner lifts the arm to 90° of abduction and asks the patient to lower it slowly to the side

cards.back: The patient raises the arm slowly through abduction in the scapular plane while the examiner watches the arc and asks where it hurts

cards.front: What is a positive Painful arc?

cards.front: What does a positive Painful arc suggest?
cards.back: A subacromial pain syndrome or rotator cuff-related shoulder pain; pain only at the very top of the arc points to the AC joint

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the Painful arc?
cards.back: Scapular dyskinesis, fear of movement or a stiff joint can change the arc; pain at the very top is not the same finding

cards.front: What does the Neer impingement test look for?
cards.back: Pain from the subacromial space when the arm is raised to end range

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the Neer impingement test?
cards.back: Sitting or standing; examiner beside the patient with one hand stopping the scapula from rotating

cards.back: With the arm turned inwards, the examiner raises the arm passively in the scapular plane to the end of range while holding the scapula down

cards.front: What does a positive Neer impingement test suggest?
cards.back: Pain from the rotator cuff or subacromial bursa (subacromial pain syndrome)

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the Neer impingement test?
cards.back: Any painful shoulder can hurt at the end of elevation, so the test is not specific; AC joint or biceps pain can mimic it

cards.front: What does the Hawkins-Kennedy test look for?

cards.front: What does a positive Hawkins-Kennedy test suggest?
cards.back: Subacromial pain syndrome or rotator cuff-related shoulder pain

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the Hawkins-Kennedy test?
cards.back: Pain from the AC joint, biceps tendon or a stiff capsule gives the same answer; do not push into pain that is severe
