cards.front: What does the Drop-arm test look for?
cards.back: Large rotator cuff tear (supraspinatus)

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the Drop-arm test?
cards.back: Standing or sitting; examiner behind or beside the patient

cards.front: How is the Drop-arm test performed?
cards.back: The examiner lifts the arm to 90° of abduction and asks the patient to lower it slowly to the side

cards.front: What is a positive Drop-arm test?
cards.back: The arm drops suddenly or the patient cannot lower it smoothly, usually with pain

cards.front: What does a positive Drop-arm test suggest?
cards.back: A large, full-thickness supraspinatus tear

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the Drop-arm test?
cards.back: Pain can cause a sudden drop; a partial tear or tendinopathy usually passes the test

cards.front: What does the Hornblower's sign look for?
cards.back: Teres minor (and infraspinatus) function

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the Hornblower's sign?
cards.back: Sitting; arm raised to 90° in the scapular plane, elbow bent to 90°

cards.front: How is the Hornblower's sign performed?
cards.back: The examiner supports the arm and asks the patient to rotate the forearm outwards against light resistance, as if lifting a horn to the mouth

cards.front: What is a positive Hornblower's sign?
cards.back: The patient cannot hold the outward rotation and the forearm drops into internal rotation

cards.front: What does a positive Hornblower's sign suggest?
cards.back: A massive posterior rotator cuff tear involving teres minor

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the Hornblower's sign?
cards.back: Pain or poor elevation range can stop the patient reaching the position

cards.front: What does the Belly-press test look for?
cards.back: Subscapularis function

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the Belly-press test?
cards.back: Standing or sitting; hand flat on the belly with the elbow in front of the body

cards.front: How is the Belly-press test performed?
cards.back: The patient presses the hand into the belly while keeping the wrist straight and the elbow forward; the examiner may try to pull the hand away

cards.front: What is a positive Belly-press test?
cards.back: The elbow drops backwards, the wrist flexes or the patient cannot press

cards.front: What does a positive Belly-press test suggest?
cards.back: A subscapularis tear or weakness

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the Belly-press test?
cards.back: Pain, a tight chest or a weak patient can fail the test for other reasons; the elbow must stay in front

cards.front: What does the Lift-off test (Gerber) look for?
cards.back: Subscapularis tear

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the Lift-off test (Gerber)?
cards.back: Standing or sitting; the back of the hand against the lower back

cards.front: How is the Lift-off test (Gerber) performed?
cards.back: The patient lifts the hand away from the back against the examiner's resistance

cards.front: What is a positive Lift-off test (Gerber)?
cards.back: The patient cannot lift the hand off the back

cards.front: What does a positive Lift-off test (Gerber) suggest?
cards.back: A subscapularis tear

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the Lift-off test (Gerber)?
cards.back: Needs enough internal rotation and extension to reach the start position, so it is often impossible when the shoulder is painful or stiff

cards.front: What does the Speed's test look for?
cards.back: Long head of biceps tendon pain, and labral pathology (SLAP)

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the Speed's test?
cards.back: Standing or sitting; arm forward to 90°, elbow straight, palm up

cards.front: How is the Speed's test performed?
cards.back: The patient resists the examiner's downward pressure on the arm

cards.front: What is a positive Speed's test?
cards.back: Pain in the bicipital groove at the front of the shoulder

cards.front: What does a positive Speed's test suggest?
cards.back: Biceps tendinopathy or a labral problem

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the Speed's test?
cards.back: Pain from the subacromial space during elevation can be mistaken for biceps pain

cards.front: What does the Yergason's test look for?
cards.back: Biceps tendon pain or instability in the bicipital groove

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the Yergason's test?
cards.back: Sitting; elbow bent to 90° and held against the side, forearm pronated

cards.front: How is the Yergason's test performed?
cards.back: The patient supinates the forearm and rotates the shoulder outwards against the examiner's resistance

cards.front: What is a positive Yergason's test?
cards.back: Pain in the bicipital groove, or the tendon felt to click out of the groove

cards.front: What does a positive Yergason's test suggest?
cards.back: Biceps tendinopathy or a subluxing tendon

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the Yergason's test?
cards.back: Resisted movement can provoke other shoulder structures; the groove must be palpated to confirm the source

cards.front: What does the O'Brien active compression test look for?
cards.back: Labral (SLAP) tear and AC joint pain

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the O'Brien active compression test?
cards.back: Standing; arm forward to 90°, a little across the body, thumb down

cards.front: How is the O'Brien active compression test performed?
cards.back: The patient resists a downward force; the test is repeated with the palm facing up

cards.front: What is a positive O'Brien active compression test?
cards.back: Pain or a click deep inside the shoulder that is relieved with the palm up

cards.front: What does a positive O'Brien active compression test suggest?
cards.back: A labral tear if the pain is deep inside the joint; the AC joint if the pain is on top of the shoulder

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the O'Brien active compression test?
cards.back: Accuracy for SLAP lesions is only fair and varies between studies; other painful shoulders can give a false positive

cards.front: What does the Apprehension and relocation test look for?
cards.back: Anterior glenohumeral instability

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the Apprehension and relocation test?
cards.back: Supine; shoulder abducted to 90° and the elbow bent to 90°

cards.front: How is the Apprehension and relocation test performed?
cards.back: The examiner slowly rotates the shoulder outwards; if apprehension appears, a backward force on the humeral head is applied and the apprehension should ease

cards.front: What is a positive Apprehension and relocation test?
cards.back: A feeling that the shoulder will come out (apprehension), relieved by the relocating force

cards.front: What does a positive Apprehension and relocation test suggest?
cards.back: Anterior shoulder instability

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the Apprehension and relocation test?
cards.back: Pain alone is not a positive test; the patient must show true apprehension. Stop before the shoulder is forced out

cards.front: What does the Sulcus sign look for?
cards.back: Inferior glenohumeral laxity (multidirectional instability)

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the Sulcus sign?
cards.back: Sitting or standing with the arm relaxed by the side

cards.front: How is the Sulcus sign performed?
cards.back: The examiner pulls the arm downwards by the elbow or wrist and watches the space below the acromion

cards.front: What is a positive Sulcus sign?
cards.back: A visible gap (sulcus) appears below the acromion, graded by its depth; a sulcus that does not close in external rotation suggests rotator interval laxity

cards.front: What does a positive Sulcus sign suggest?
cards.back: Inferior laxity, as in multidirectional instability or generalised hypermobility

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the Sulcus sign?
cards.back: Many healthy people with generalised laxity show a small sulcus; always compare with the other side

cards.front: What does the Load and shift test look for?
cards.back: Anterior and posterior glenohumeral laxity

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the Load and shift test?
cards.back: Sitting or lying; examiner holds the scapula and clavicle with one hand and the humeral head with the other

cards.front: How is the Load and shift test performed?
cards.back: The humeral head is pressed lightly into the socket (load) and then moved forwards and backwards (shift), and the amount of movement is graded

cards.front: What is a positive Load and shift test?
cards.back: More translation than the other side, or the head rides to the rim of the socket or over it

cards.front: What does a positive Load and shift test suggest?
cards.back: Glenohumeral laxity in the direction tested

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the Load and shift test?
cards.back: Muscle guarding hides laxity; laxity is not the same as instability

cards.front: What does the Cross-body adduction test look for?
cards.back: Acromioclavicular (AC) joint pain

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the Cross-body adduction test?
cards.back: Sitting or standing; arm raised to 90° forward

cards.front: How is the Cross-body adduction test performed?
cards.back: The examiner moves the arm passively across the chest into horizontal adduction

cards.front: What is a positive Cross-body adduction test?
cards.back: Pain on top of the shoulder at the AC joint

cards.front: What does a positive Cross-body adduction test suggest?
cards.back: AC joint arthritis or sprain

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the Cross-body adduction test?
cards.back: Pain at the back of the shoulder may be posterior capsule tightness, not the AC joint

cards.front: What does the Cozen's test look for?
cards.back: Lateral epicondylalgia (tennis elbow)

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the Cozen's test?
cards.back: Sitting; elbow bent and supported, forearm turned palm down

cards.front: How is the Cozen's test performed?
cards.back: The patient makes a fist and extends the wrist against the examiner's resistance

cards.front: What is a positive Cozen's test?
cards.back: Sharp pain over the lateral epicondyle

cards.front: What does a positive Cozen's test suggest?
cards.back: Tendinopathy of the common wrist extensor origin (lateral epicondylalgia)

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the Cozen's test?
cards.back: Pain from the neck or the radial tunnel can reach the same area

cards.front: What does the Mill's test look for?
cards.back: Lateral epicondylalgia (tennis elbow)

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the Mill's test?
cards.back: Sitting; elbow straight, forearm turned palm down

cards.front: How is the Mill's test performed?
cards.back: The examiner flexes the patient's wrist fully while the elbow stays straight, stretching the wrist extensors

cards.front: What is a positive Mill's test?
cards.back: Pain over the lateral epicondyle

cards.front: What does a positive Mill's test suggest?
cards.back: Lateral epicondylalgia

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the Mill's test?
cards.back: Do not force the stretch into severe pain; a stiff wrist can give a false answer

cards.front: What does the Resisted wrist flexion test look for?
cards.back: Medial epicondylalgia (golfer's elbow)

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the Resisted wrist flexion test?
cards.back: Sitting; elbow straight and forearm turned palm up

cards.front: How is the Resisted wrist flexion test performed?
cards.back: The patient flexes the wrist against the examiner's resistance

cards.front: What is a positive Resisted wrist flexion test?
cards.back: Pain over the medial epicondyle

cards.front: What does a positive Resisted wrist flexion test suggest?
cards.back: Tendinopathy of the common wrist flexor origin

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the Resisted wrist flexion test?
cards.back: Ulnar nerve irritation at the elbow can also cause medial pain and tingling

cards.front: What does the Valgus stress test (elbow) look for?
cards.back: Medial (ulnar) collateral ligament laxity

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the Valgus stress test (elbow)?
cards.back: Sitting or supine; elbow bent to 20°-30° with the forearm turned palm up

cards.front: How is the Valgus stress test (elbow) performed?
cards.back: The examiner stabilises the upper arm and pushes the forearm outwards, opening the inner side of the joint

cards.front: What is a positive Valgus stress test (elbow)?
cards.back: Pain or more opening than the other side, with a soft end-point

cards.front: What does a positive Valgus stress test (elbow) suggest?
cards.back: A sprain or tear of the medial collateral ligament, common in throwers

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the Valgus stress test (elbow)?
cards.back: Testing with the elbow straight lets the bone lock the joint and hide laxity

cards.front: What does the Varus stress test (elbow) look for?
cards.back: Lateral collateral ligament laxity

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the Varus stress test (elbow)?
cards.back: Sitting or supine; elbow bent to 20°-30°

cards.front: How is the Varus stress test (elbow) performed?
cards.back: The examiner stabilises the upper arm and pushes the forearm inwards, opening the outer side of the joint

cards.front: What is a positive Varus stress test (elbow)?
cards.back: Pain or more opening than the other side, with a soft end-point

cards.front: What does a positive Varus stress test (elbow) suggest?
cards.back: A lateral collateral ligament sprain or posterolateral instability after dislocation

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the Varus stress test (elbow)?
cards.back: Testing in full extension hides laxity; shoulder rotation changes the feel

cards.front: What does the Elbow flexion test look for?
cards.back: Ulnar nerve compression at the cubital tunnel

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the Elbow flexion test?
cards.back: Sitting; arms by the side

cards.front: How is the Elbow flexion test performed?
cards.back: The patient holds the elbow fully bent with the wrist extended for up to about one minute

cards.front: What is a positive Elbow flexion test?
cards.back: Tingling or numbness in the ring and little finger within the minute

cards.front: What does a positive Elbow flexion test suggest?
cards.back: Cubital tunnel syndrome (ulnar nerve entrapment at the elbow)

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the Elbow flexion test?
cards.back: Some healthy people have tingling with sustained elbow flexion; tap over the nerve as well (Tinel's) and compare both sides

cards.front: What does the Phalen's test look for?
cards.back: Carpal tunnel syndrome (median nerve)

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the Phalen's test?
cards.back: Sitting; elbows resting on a table

cards.front: How is the Phalen's test performed?
cards.back: The patient presses the backs of the hands together (wrists flexed) for up to 60 seconds

cards.front: What is a positive Phalen's test?
cards.back: Tingling or numbness in the thumb, index and middle fingers

cards.front: What does a positive Phalen's test suggest?
cards.back: Median nerve compression in the carpal tunnel

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the Phalen's test?
cards.back: Healthy people may feel mild tingling; stop at once if symptoms are strong

cards.front: What does the Tinel's sign at the wrist look for?
cards.back: Irritable median nerve at the carpal tunnel

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the Tinel's sign at the wrist?
cards.back: Sitting; forearm supported with the palm up

cards.front: How is the Tinel's sign at the wrist performed?
cards.back: The examiner taps lightly over the median nerve at the front of the wrist

cards.front: What is a positive Tinel's sign at the wrist?
cards.back: Tingling shooting into the thumb, index and middle fingers

cards.front: What does a positive Tinel's sign at the wrist suggest?
cards.back: Median nerve irritation in the carpal tunnel

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the Tinel's sign at the wrist?
cards.back: A heavy tap causes tingling in anyone; tap lightly and compare with the other wrist

cards.front: What does the Carpal compression test look for?
cards.back: Carpal tunnel syndrome

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the Carpal compression test?
cards.back: Sitting; forearm supported with the palm up

cards.front: How is the Carpal compression test performed?
cards.back: The examiner presses firmly with both thumbs over the carpal tunnel for up to 30 seconds

cards.front: What is a positive Carpal compression test?
cards.back: Tingling or numbness in the median nerve distribution

cards.front: What does a positive Carpal compression test suggest?
cards.back: Median nerve compression at the carpal tunnel

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the Carpal compression test?
cards.back: Pressing on the wrong place (over the tendons) or pressing very hard gives false results

cards.front: What does the Finkelstein's test look for?
cards.back: De Quervain's tenosynovitis

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the Finkelstein's test?
cards.back: Sitting; forearm resting on the table with the hand in the neutral position

cards.front: How is the Finkelstein's test performed?
cards.back: The patient folds the thumb into the palm under the fingers; the wrist is then moved into ulnar deviation

cards.front: What is a positive Finkelstein's test?
cards.back: Sharp pain over the radial side of the wrist at the first dorsal compartment

cards.front: What does a positive Finkelstein's test suggest?
cards.back: Inflammation of the abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis tendons

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the Finkelstein's test?
cards.back: Pain at the base of the thumb with grinding suggests thumb joint arthritis, not De Quervain's

cards.front: What does the Watson scaphoid shift test look for?
cards.back: Scapholunate ligament instability

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the Watson scaphoid shift test?
cards.back: Sitting; the examiner holds the wrist with the thumb on the scaphoid tubercle

cards.front: How is the Watson scaphoid shift test performed?
cards.back: While pressing the scaphoid, the examiner moves the wrist from ulnar to radial deviation and releases the pressure

cards.front: What is a positive Watson scaphoid shift test?
cards.back: A painful clunk as the scaphoid slips over the rim of the radius

cards.front: What does a positive Watson scaphoid shift test suggest?
cards.back: Scapholunate dissociation

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the Watson scaphoid shift test?
cards.back: Many healthy wrists have laxity and a click; look for pain and a difference from the other wrist

cards.front: What does the Froment's sign look for?
cards.back: Ulnar nerve weakness of the thumb adductor

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the Froment's sign?
cards.back: Sitting; a flat piece of paper held between the thumb and the side of the index finger

cards.front: How is the Froment's sign performed?
cards.back: The examiner tries to pull the paper out while the patient grips it with straight thumbs

cards.front: What is a positive Froment's sign?
cards.back: The thumb tip joint bends to keep hold of the paper

cards.front: What does a positive Froment's sign suggest?
cards.back: Weakness of adductor pollicis from an ulnar nerve lesion; flexor pollicis longus is compensating

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the Froment's sign?
cards.back: Pain or a stiff thumb can produce the same posture; compare both hands

cards.front: What does the Thumb carpometacarpal grind test look for?
cards.back: Osteoarthritis of the thumb base

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the Thumb carpometacarpal grind test?
cards.back: Sitting; forearm supported

cards.front: How is the Thumb carpometacarpal grind test performed?
cards.back: The examiner presses the thumb metacarpal into the joint (axial load) and rotates it

cards.front: What is a positive Thumb carpometacarpal grind test?
cards.back: Pain and sometimes grinding at the base of the thumb

cards.front: What does a positive Thumb carpometacarpal grind test suggest?
cards.back: Arthritis of the first carpometacarpal joint

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the Thumb carpometacarpal grind test?
cards.back: Pain from De Quervain's tenosynovitis lies higher, over the radial styloid

cards.front: What does the Scaphoid fracture tests look for?
cards.back: Possible scaphoid fracture after a fall on the hand

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the Scaphoid fracture tests?
cards.back: Sitting; wrist supported

cards.front: How is the Scaphoid fracture tests performed?
cards.back: Press the anatomical snuffbox, press the scaphoid tubercle at the base of the thumb on the palm side, and compress the thumb along its length

cards.front: What is a positive Scaphoid fracture tests?
cards.back: Pain at the snuffbox or tubercle, or pain on compression of the thumb

cards.front: What does a positive Scaphoid fracture tests suggest?
cards.back: A possible scaphoid fracture, which may not show on the first X-ray

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the Scaphoid fracture tests?
cards.back: An early normal X-ray does not exclude a fracture; delay in diagnosis risks non-union and avascular necrosis

cards.front: What does the FABER (Patrick) test look for?
cards.back: Hip joint, sacroiliac joint and hip muscle pain

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the FABER (Patrick) test?
cards.back: Supine; the foot of the tested leg rests on the opposite knee

cards.front: How is the FABER (Patrick) test performed?
cards.back: The examiner presses the bent knee down towards the table while holding the opposite hip steady

cards.front: What is a positive FABER (Patrick) test?
cards.back: Groin pain (hip joint), or pain over the back of the pelvis (sacroiliac joint), or a clearly smaller range than the other side

cards.front: What does a positive FABER (Patrick) test suggest?
cards.back: Hip joint pathology if the pain is in the groin; sacroiliac joint if the pain is behind

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the FABER (Patrick) test?
cards.back: Pain location matters: the same test can be positive for the hip or the pelvis. Do not push into severe pain

cards.front: What does the FADIR test look for?
cards.back: Femoroacetabular impingement and labral irritation

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the FADIR test?
cards.back: Supine

cards.front: How is the FADIR test performed?
cards.back: The hip is bent to about 90°, then adducted and turned inwards (internal rotation) by the examiner

cards.front: What is a positive FADIR test?
cards.back: Pain in the groin that matches the patient's usual pain

cards.front: What does a positive FADIR test suggest?
cards.back: An intra-articular hip problem such as femoroacetabular impingement or a labral tear

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the FADIR test?
cards.back: Pain from muscles, the pubic area or the lower back can mimic groin pain

cards.front: What does the Hip scour (quadrant) test look for?
cards.back: Intra-articular hip pain and cartilage or labral damage

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the Hip scour (quadrant) test?
cards.back: Supine

cards.front: How is the Hip scour (quadrant) test performed?
cards.back: The hip is bent to 90° and the examiner presses along the thigh while moving the hip in an arc from adduction to abduction

cards.front: What is a positive Hip scour (quadrant) test?
cards.back: Pain, catching or grinding in the groin or hip

cards.front: What does a positive Hip scour (quadrant) test suggest?
cards.back: An intra-articular hip problem such as arthritis or a labral tear

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the Hip scour (quadrant) test?
cards.back: Compression through a very painful hip can be stopped early; do not force it

cards.front: What does the Log roll test look for?
cards.back: Pain from within the hip joint

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the Log roll test?
cards.back: Supine with the legs straight and relaxed

cards.front: How is the Log roll test performed?
cards.back: The examiner rolls the whole leg inwards and outwards by moving the thigh, keeping the muscles relaxed

cards.front: What is a positive Log roll test?
cards.back: Groin pain or a reduced or guarded rolling movement

cards.front: What does a positive Log roll test suggest?
cards.back: An intra-articular hip problem (arthritis, fracture or infection in the right setting)

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the Log roll test?
cards.back: Muscle spasm can make rolling feel stiff; do not use it to exclude a fracture after a fall

cards.front: What does the Resisted straight leg raise (Stinchfield) look for?
cards.back: Intra-articular hip pain under load

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the Resisted straight leg raise (Stinchfield)?
cards.back: Supine with the leg straight

cards.front: How is the Resisted straight leg raise (Stinchfield) performed?
cards.back: The patient lifts the leg to about 30° and holds it against the examiner's downward pressure

cards.front: What is a positive Resisted straight leg raise (Stinchfield)?
cards.back: Groin pain

cards.front: What does a positive Resisted straight leg raise (Stinchfield) suggest?
cards.back: An intra-articular hip problem

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the Resisted straight leg raise (Stinchfield)?
cards.back: Hip flexor or abdominal pain can be mistaken for hip pain; note where the pain is

cards.front: What does the Trendelenburg test look for?
cards.back: Hip abductor (gluteus medius) function

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the Trendelenburg test?
cards.back: Standing, barefoot, facing away from the examiner who watches the pelvis from behind

cards.front: How is the Trendelenburg test performed?
cards.back: The patient stands on one leg for about 30 seconds while the examiner watches the pelvis and trunk

cards.front: What is a positive Trendelenburg test?
cards.back: The pelvis drops on the side of the lifted leg, or the trunk leans over the standing leg to compensate

cards.front: What does a positive Trendelenburg test suggest?
cards.back: Weakness or poor control of the gluteus medius of the standing leg

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the Trendelenburg test?
cards.back: Pain, poor balance or a short leg can create a false drop; a trunk lean (compensated Trendelenburg) is also a positive sign

cards.front: What does the Lachman test look for?
cards.back: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) rupture

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the Lachman test?
cards.back: Supine; knee bent to 20° to 30°, the examiner's one hand holds the thigh and the other the upper tibia

cards.front: How is the Lachman test performed?
cards.back: The examiner pulls the tibia forward on the femur and judges the amount of movement and the feel of the end-point

cards.front: What is a positive Lachman test?
cards.back: More forward movement than the other side with a soft or missing end-point

cards.front: What does a positive Lachman test suggest?
cards.back: A torn ACL

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the Lachman test?
cards.back: A knee bent too far, muscle guarding, a thigh too heavy to hold or a swollen painful knee all reduce accuracy

cards.front: What does the Anterior drawer test (knee) look for?
cards.back: ACL rupture

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the Anterior drawer test (knee)?
cards.back: Supine; hip bent to 45° and knee to 90°, the examiner sits lightly on the foot

cards.front: How is the Anterior drawer test (knee) performed?
cards.back: With the hamstrings relaxed, the examiner pulls the upper tibia forward and compares the movement with the other side

cards.front: What is a positive Anterior drawer test (knee)?
cards.back: More forward movement than the other side, with a soft end-point

cards.front: What does a positive Anterior drawer test (knee) suggest?
cards.back: A torn ACL

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the Anterior drawer test (knee)?
cards.back: Guarding from pain or swelling hides laxity; start with the posterior sag so a posterior tibial sag is not mistaken for forward movement

cards.front: What does the Posterior drawer and sag sign look for?
cards.back: Posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) rupture

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the Posterior drawer and sag sign?
cards.back: Supine; hip bent to 45° and knee to 90°, feet flat on the table

cards.front: How is the Posterior drawer and sag sign performed?
cards.back: Look from the side for a sag of the upper tibia (sag sign), then push the tibia backwards with both thumbs on the joint line

cards.front: What is a positive Posterior drawer and sag sign?
cards.back: The tibia sags backwards or moves further back than the other side with a soft end-point

cards.front: What does a positive Posterior drawer and sag sign suggest?
cards.back: A torn PCL

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the Posterior drawer and sag sign?
cards.back: A sag that is not noticed can be mistaken for an anterior drawer, creating a false ACL finding

cards.front: What does the Pivot shift test look for?
cards.back: Rotatory instability from an ACL tear

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the Pivot shift test?
cards.back: Supine; the examiner holds the foot and the outer knee

cards.front: How is the Pivot shift test performed?
cards.back: With the leg straight and turned inwards, a valgus force is applied while the knee is gradually bent

cards.front: What is a positive Pivot shift test?
cards.back: The tibia clunks or slips back into place at about 20° to 40° of flexion

cards.front: What does a positive Pivot shift test suggest?
cards.back: A torn ACL with rotatory instability

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the Pivot shift test?
cards.back: An awake patient often guards, so a normal result does not exclude a tear

cards.front: What does the McMurray test look for?
cards.back: Meniscal tear

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the McMurray test?
cards.back: Supine; knee fully bent, the examiner holds the heel and the joint line

cards.front: How is the McMurray test performed?
cards.back: The examiner turns the lower leg outwards with a valgus force (medial meniscus), or inwards with a varus force (lateral meniscus), then straightens the knee

cards.front: What is a positive McMurray test?
cards.back: A painful click or pain along the joint line

cards.front: What does a positive McMurray test suggest?
cards.back: A tear of the meniscus on the side tested

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the McMurray test?
cards.back: Pain from arthritis or the patella can mimic it; some tears produce no click

cards.front: What does the Thessaly test look for?
cards.back: Meniscal tear under weight-bearing load

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the Thessaly test?
cards.back: Standing on the injured leg with the knee slightly bent (20°), holding the examiner's hands

cards.front: How is the Thessaly test performed?
cards.back: The patient twists the knee and body inwards and outwards three times while the knee stays bent

cards.front: What is a positive Thessaly test?
cards.back: Joint line pain, catching or a feeling that the knee will lock

cards.front: What does a positive Thessaly test suggest?
cards.back: A meniscal tear

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the Thessaly test?
cards.back: Reported accuracy was high in the first study and lower in later ones; weak or painful patients may not manage it

cards.front: What does the Valgus stress test (knee) look for?
cards.back: Medial collateral ligament (MCL) sprain or tear

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the Valgus stress test (knee)?
cards.back: Supine; the knee is tested straight and again at 30° of flexion

cards.front: How is the Valgus stress test (knee) performed?
cards.back: The examiner supports the leg and pushes the knee inwards (valgus) while pulling the ankle outwards

cards.front: What is a positive Valgus stress test (knee)?
cards.back: Pain, more opening of the inner joint line than the other side, or a soft end-point

cards.front: What does a positive Valgus stress test (knee) suggest?
cards.back: An MCL injury; laxity at 30° alone suggests the MCL, laxity also when straight suggests the cruciate or capsule are involved

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the Valgus stress test (knee)?
cards.back: Rotation of the leg, or muscle guarding, changes the findings; the grade depends on the opening and the end-point

cards.front: What does the Varus stress test (knee) look for?
cards.back: Lateral collateral ligament (LCL) and posterolateral corner injury

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the Varus stress test (knee)?
cards.back: Supine; the knee is tested straight and again at 30° of flexion

cards.front: How is the Varus stress test (knee) performed?
cards.back: The examiner pushes the knee outwards (varus) while pulling the ankle inwards

cards.front: What is a positive Varus stress test (knee)?
cards.back: Pain or more opening of the outer joint line than the other side

cards.front: What does a positive Varus stress test (knee) suggest?
cards.back: An LCL injury; laxity when straight suggests the posterolateral corner or cruciate ligaments are involved

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the Varus stress test (knee)?
cards.back: Hip rotation and muscle guarding change the result; compare with the other leg

cards.front: What does the Patellar apprehension test look for?
cards.back: Patellar instability

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the Patellar apprehension test?
cards.back: Supine; knee relaxed and slightly bent (20° to 30°)

cards.front: How is the Patellar apprehension test performed?
cards.back: The examiner pushes the patella gently outwards

cards.front: What is a positive Patellar apprehension test?
cards.back: The patient looks worried, tenses the thigh or stops the movement to avoid a dislocation

cards.front: What does a positive Patellar apprehension test suggest?
cards.back: Patellar instability, typically after a previous dislocation

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the Patellar apprehension test?
cards.back: Pain alone is not a positive test; apprehension must be shown

cards.front: What does the Effusion tests (sweep and patellar tap) look for?
cards.back: Fluid inside the knee joint

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the Effusion tests (sweep and patellar tap)?
cards.back: Supine with the knee straight and the quadriceps relaxed

cards.front: How is the Effusion tests (sweep and patellar tap) performed?
cards.back: Sweep: stroke fluid up the inner side and then down the outer side and watch for a bulge. Patellar tap: squeeze fluid out of the pouch above the knee and tap the patella down

cards.front: What is a positive Effusion tests (sweep and patellar tap)?
cards.back: A bulge on the inner side after the sweep, or a tap felt as the patella floats and hits the femur

cards.front: What does a positive Effusion tests (sweep and patellar tap) suggest?
cards.back: A knee effusion; swelling within a few hours of an injury suggests bleeding into the joint (haemarthrosis)

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the Effusion tests (sweep and patellar tap)?
cards.back: The sweep detects small amounts, the tap needs a larger effusion; a tight, overweight or very muscular knee is difficult to read

cards.front: What does the Ottawa knee rule look for?
cards.back: Deciding whether an X-ray is needed after an acute knee injury

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the Ottawa knee rule?
cards.back: Any position; examine and ask the patient to walk

cards.front: How is the Ottawa knee rule performed?
cards.back: Check the five items: age 55 or more, tenderness of the head of the fibula, isolated tenderness of the patella, inability to bend the knee to 90°, and inability to take four steps both at the time of injury and now

cards.front: What is a positive Ottawa knee rule?
cards.back: Any one of the five items

cards.front: What does a positive Ottawa knee rule suggest?
cards.back: An X-ray is needed to look for a fracture

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the Ottawa knee rule?
cards.back: The rule is for acute injuries and was developed for adults; it does not exclude ligament or meniscus injury

cards.front: What does the Anterior drawer test (ankle) look for?
cards.back: Anterior talofibular ligament (ATFL) sprain or tear

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the Anterior drawer test (ankle)?
cards.back: Sitting with the knee bent or supine; ankle relaxed in about 10° to 20° of plantarflexion

cards.front: How is the Anterior drawer test (ankle) performed?
cards.back: The examiner holds the lower leg still and pulls the heel forward, comparing the movement and the end-point with the other ankle

cards.front: What is a positive Anterior drawer test (ankle)?
cards.back: More forward movement than the other side, a soft end-point or a dimple in front of the lateral malleolus (suction sign)

cards.front: What does a positive Anterior drawer test (ankle) suggest?
cards.back: An ATFL sprain or rupture

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the Anterior drawer test (ankle)?
cards.back: Swelling and pain in the first days hide laxity; ankle too far plantarflexed or the leg not held still

cards.front: What does the Talar tilt (inversion stress) test look for?
cards.back: Calcaneofibular ligament (CFL) and ATFL laxity

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the Talar tilt (inversion stress) test?
cards.back: Sitting or supine; ankle in neutral

cards.front: How is the Talar tilt (inversion stress) test performed?
cards.back: The examiner holds the lower leg and tilts the heel inwards (inversion), comparing the tilt with the other ankle

cards.front: What is a positive Talar tilt (inversion stress) test?
cards.back: More tilt than the other side or pain over the lateral ligaments

cards.front: What does a positive Talar tilt (inversion stress) test suggest?
cards.back: A CFL sprain or tear, often with the ATFL

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the Talar tilt (inversion stress) test?
cards.back: Pain guarding, and normal differences between ankles, can change the result

cards.front: What does the Squeeze test (syndesmosis) look for?
cards.back: Injury of the syndesmosis (high ankle sprain)

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the Squeeze test (syndesmosis)?
cards.back: Sitting or supine; leg relaxed

cards.front: How is the Squeeze test (syndesmosis) performed?
cards.back: The examiner squeezes the tibia and fibula together at the middle of the calf, and watches for pain at the ankle

cards.front: What is a positive Squeeze test (syndesmosis)?
cards.back: Pain at the front of the ankle between the tibia and fibula, far from the squeeze

cards.front: What does a positive Squeeze test (syndesmosis) suggest?
cards.back: A syndesmosis injury

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the Squeeze test (syndesmosis)?
cards.back: Pain at the squeeze site is not a positive result; the pain must appear at the ankle

cards.front: What does the External rotation (Kleiger) test look for?
cards.back: Syndesmosis and deltoid ligament injury

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the External rotation (Kleiger) test?
cards.back: Sitting with the knee bent to 90°; ankle in neutral

cards.front: How is the External rotation (Kleiger) test performed?
cards.back: The examiner holds the leg still and turns the foot outwards

cards.front: What is a positive External rotation (Kleiger) test?
cards.back: Pain at the syndesmosis in front of the ankle, or at the inner side of the ankle

cards.front: What does a positive External rotation (Kleiger) test suggest?
cards.back: A syndesmosis sprain or a deltoid ligament sprain

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the External rotation (Kleiger) test?
cards.back: Too much force can aggravate a painful ankle; compare with the other side

cards.front: What does the Thompson (calf squeeze) test look for?
cards.back: Achilles tendon rupture

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the Thompson (calf squeeze) test?
cards.back: Lying face down with the feet over the end of the bed, or kneeling on a chair

cards.front: How is the Thompson (calf squeeze) test performed?
cards.back: The examiner squeezes the calf and watches the foot

cards.front: What is a positive Thompson (calf squeeze) test?
cards.back: The foot does not point down (no plantarflexion) when the calf is squeezed

cards.front: What does a positive Thompson (calf squeeze) test suggest?
cards.back: A complete rupture of the Achilles tendon

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the Thompson (calf squeeze) test?
cards.back: Other plantarflexors can move the foot a little; a partial tear can give a normal result

cards.front: What does the Windlass test look for?
cards.back: Plantar heel pain from the plantar fascia

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the Windlass test?
cards.back: Standing or with the foot hanging over the edge of the bed

cards.front: How is the Windlass test performed?
cards.back: The examiner extends the big toe at the first joint, tightening the plantar fascia

cards.front: What is a positive Windlass test?
cards.back: The patient's heel or arch pain is reproduced

cards.front: What does a positive Windlass test suggest?
cards.back: Plantar fasciopathy (plantar heel pain)

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the Windlass test?
cards.back: Pain from the big toe joint itself can be confused with heel pain; note where it hurts

cards.front: What does the Metatarsal squeeze (Mulder's click) look for?
cards.back: Morton's neuroma and metatarsalgia

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the Metatarsal squeeze (Mulder's click)?
cards.back: Sitting or supine; the foot is held in the examiner's hand

cards.front: How is the Metatarsal squeeze (Mulder's click) performed?
cards.back: The examiner squeezes the metatarsal heads together while pressing the web space between the toes

cards.front: What is a positive Metatarsal squeeze (Mulder's click)?
cards.back: Pain or a click between the toes, with tingling or burning into the toes

cards.front: What does a positive Metatarsal squeeze (Mulder's click) suggest?
cards.back: An interdigital (Morton's) neuroma

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the Metatarsal squeeze (Mulder's click)?
cards.back: Joint pain between the metatarsals can look similar; a click alone is not enough

cards.front: What does the Ottawa ankle rules look for?
cards.back: Deciding whether an X-ray is needed after an ankle or midfoot injury

cards.front: How are the patient and the examiner positioned for the Ottawa ankle rules?
cards.back: Examine the bones and ask the patient to walk four steps

cards.front: How is the Ottawa ankle rules performed?
cards.back: Ankle X-ray if there is pain near the ankle and bone tenderness at the back edge or tip of either malleolus, or inability to take four steps. Foot X-ray if there is midfoot pain with tenderness at the base of the fifth metatarsal or the navicular, or inability to take four steps

cards.front: What is a positive Ottawa ankle rules?
cards.back: Any of those findings

cards.front: What does a positive Ottawa ankle rules suggest?
cards.back: An X-ray is needed to look for a fracture

cards.front: Common pitfalls of the Ottawa ankle rules?
cards.back: The rules were made for adults with acute injuries and do not rule out ligament injury

cards.front: A very sensitive test is negative. What is it best at?
cards.back: Ruling the problem out. A highly sensitive test misses few people with the problem, so a negative result helps to rule it out (SnNout).

cards.front: Which is the best single clinical test for an ACL rupture?
cards.back: Lachman test. The Lachman test is the most accurate single clinical test for the ACL.

cards.front: Phalen's test is used to assess which problem?
cards.back: Carpal tunnel syndrome. Sustained wrist flexion tests for median nerve compression in the carpal tunnel.

cards.front: What is a positive Thompson test?
cards.back: No plantarflexion when the calf is squeezed. No movement of the foot on a calf squeeze suggests a complete Achilles rupture.

cards.front: Finkelstein's test looks for which condition?
cards.back: De Quervain's tenosynovitis. Ulnar deviation with the thumb in the palm stretches the first dorsal compartment tendons.

cards.front: Which movements make up the FADIR position?
cards.back: Flexion, adduction and internal rotation. FADIR stands for flexion, adduction and internal rotation.

cards.front: In a positive Trendelenburg test the pelvis drops on which side?
cards.back: The side of the lifted leg. The pelvis falls on the lifted side because the gluteus medius of the standing leg cannot hold it level.

cards.front: Cozen's test is a resisted movement of which kind?
cards.back: Wrist extension. Resisted wrist extension loads the extensor origin at the lateral epicondyle.

cards.front: The sulcus sign points to which problem?
cards.back: Inferior shoulder laxity. A gap below the acromion on downward traction shows inferior glenohumeral laxity.

cards.front: What are the Ottawa ankle rules for?
cards.back: Deciding if an X-ray is needed. They help decide whether an ankle or foot X-ray is needed after an acute injury.

cards.front: What is a positive apprehension test?
cards.back: The patient fears the joint will come out. Fear of dislocation, not only pain, is the positive finding.

cards.front: Why compare a test with the other side?
cards.back: Normal laxity differs between people. Each person has their own normal range; the other side is the best reference.

cards.front: At what knee angle is the Lachman test done?
cards.back: 20° to 30° of flexion. A small amount of flexion relaxes the hamstrings and lets the ACL be tested cleanly.

cards.front: A positive drop-arm test suggests tear of which tendon?
cards.back: Supraspinatus. A patient who cannot lower the abducted arm smoothly may have a large supraspinatus tear.

cards.front: Valgus laxity at 30° of knee flexion but not at 0° suggests what?
cards.back: An isolated MCL injury. At 30° the cruciates are relaxed, so laxity then points to the MCL.

cards.front: Which McMurray manoeuvre tests the lateral meniscus?
cards.back: Internal rotation with a varus force. The lower leg is turned inwards with a varus force to stress the lateral meniscus.

cards.front: A positive belly-press test suggests weakness of which muscle?
cards.back: Subscapularis. A dropped elbow or flexed wrist on pressing shows subscapularis weakness.

cards.front: Which ligament does the ankle anterior drawer test mainly assess?
cards.back: Anterior talofibular ligament. A forward pull of the heel stresses the ATFL.

cards.front: Where must the pain appear in the squeeze test to be positive?
cards.back: At the ankle, far from the squeeze. Pain between the tibia and fibula at the ankle suggests a syndesmosis injury.

cards.front: What is the position for Speed's test?
cards.back: Arm forward to 90°, elbow straight, palm up. Resisted forward elevation with the palm up loads the long head of biceps.

cards.front: The sweep test detects what?
cards.back: A small knee effusion. A bulge on the inner side after a sweep shows a small amount of fluid.

cards.front: Why is a negative pivot shift test in an awake patient not reassuring?
cards.back: Guarding hides the finding, so sensitivity is low. A clunk is strong evidence for a tear, but a negative result does not exclude it.

cards.front: A negative FADIR makes which problem less likely?
cards.back: Femoroacetabular impingement. FADIR is sensitive for intra-articular hip pain, so a negative test makes impingement less likely.

cards.front: Pain only at the very top of the painful arc suggests which structure?
cards.back: The AC joint. Pain near the end of elevation is classically an AC joint sign.

cards.front: When is the ankle anterior drawer test most accurate?
cards.back: Four to five days after the injury. Swelling and guarding settle in the first few days, so a delayed exam is more accurate.

cards.front: What does a negative McMurray test tell you?
cards.back: It does not exclude a meniscal tear. McMurray has only moderate sensitivity, so a negative test is not enough.

cards.front: Why does a syndesmosis sprain need special attention?
cards.back: It often heals more slowly than a lateral sprain. High ankle sprains take longer to settle and may need protection.

cards.front: A posterior sag of the tibia at 90° of knee flexion suggests what?
cards.back: A PCL tear. The tibia sags backwards when the PCL is torn.

cards.front: In O'Brien's test, pain relieved with the palm up suggests what?
cards.back: A labral problem. Deep pain that eases with the palm up points to the labrum, while top-of-shoulder pain points to the AC joint.

cards.front: Why combine several tests?
cards.back: Agreement between tests is stronger than one test. A cluster of tests that agree is more persuasive than any single test.

cards.front: A 24-year-old footballer twisted the knee two hours ago. The knee is swollen, painful and guarded. Lachman cannot be done. — What do you do next?
cards.back: Retest in a few days when the swelling settles, and refer for imaging. A guarded swollen knee hides laxity. Reassess after the swelling settles and image the knee.

cards.front: A 30-year-old fell on an outstretched hand. The first wrist X-ray is normal, but the anatomical snuffbox is tender and thumb compression hurts. — What is the right management?
cards.back: Treat as a fracture: immobilise and repeat or advance the imaging. Snuffbox tenderness after a fall on the hand needs immobilisation until a scaphoid fracture is excluded.

cards.front: After inverting an ankle the patient cannot take four steps and has bone tenderness at the back edge of the lateral malleolus. — What should you do first?
cards.back: Arrange an ankle X-ray. Bone tenderness at the back edge of the malleolus or inability to take four steps means an ankle X-ray under the Ottawa rules.

cards.front: While sprinting a patient felt a sudden pop in the calf. The Thompson test is positive and a gap can be felt in the tendon. — What is the appropriate action?
cards.back: Protect the leg and refer the same day. A positive Thompson test with a gap suggests a complete Achilles rupture and needs urgent referral.

cards.front: A 58-year-old has night pain, cannot hold the arm in external rotation (lag sign) and has a positive drop-arm test. — What does this suggest and what is the next step?
cards.back: A large full-thickness cuff tear; refer for imaging and specialist opinion. A lag sign and a positive drop-arm test in a person with weakness suggest a large tear that needs imaging and an orthopaedic opinion.

cards.front: A 22-year-old rugby player feels the shoulder will come out when it is abducted and turned outwards. A backward force on the humeral head relieves the feeling. — Which diagnosis is most likely?
cards.back: Anterior shoulder instability. Apprehension relieved by a relocating force in a young athlete is typical of anterior instability.

cards.front: A patient has night numbness in the hand, a positive Phalen test and a positive Tinel's sign, with wasting of the thumb muscle. — What is the best next step?
cards.back: Refer for nerve conduction studies and a specialist opinion. Thenar wasting means advanced median nerve compression and needs prompt specialist assessment.

cards.front: After a ski fall the knee opens on valgus stress both straight and at 30° with no firm end-point. — What should you suspect and do?
cards.back: A grade III MCL tear with possible cruciate injury; refer for assessment. Valgus laxity when straight and at 30° with no firm end-point suggests the cruciate ligaments or capsule are also injured.

cards.front: A 25-year-old athlete has groin pain with a positive FADIR and a positive FABER test. — Which interpretation is best?
cards.back: Possible femoroacetabular impingement; assess hip rotation and decide on imaging only if surgery is considered. Positive tests suggest an intra-articular hip problem but they are not specific; imaging is for those considering surgery.

cards.front: A patient has lateral elbow pain with a positive Cozen's test, but turning the neck also reproduces the arm pain. — What should you also examine?
cards.back: The neck, because the pain may come from the cervical spine. If arm pain is provoked by neck movement, check the cervical spine and nerve roots even when Cozen's test is positive.

cards.front: Painful arc — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: Useful but not specific. It performs best in a small cluster (painful arc, pain or weakness on resisted external rotation, Hawkins-Kennedy) rather than alone.

cards.front: Neer impingement test — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: Good at including shoulders that hurt on elevation but poor at telling which structure is at fault. Interpret with the history, the painful arc and resisted tests.

cards.front: Hawkins-Kennedy test — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: Like Neer, it is sensitive but not specific, so a negative result makes a subacromial cause less likely while a positive one does not prove it.

cards.front: Empty can (Jobe) test — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: The full can position tests the same weakness with less pain and is often preferred. Compare both sides and use it alongside the lag signs.

cards.front: External rotation lag sign — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: Specific for large tears: a clear lag is strong evidence, but its absence does not rule a tear out. Pair it with the drop-arm and the Hornblower sign.

cards.front: Drop-arm test — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: Poor sensitivity but good specificity: a positive test is meaningful, a negative one tells you little. Add the lag signs and strength testing.

cards.front: Hornblower's sign — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: A positive test points to a large tear and needs referral; it is uncommon, so a negative result is common and uninformative.

cards.front: Belly-press test — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: Easier on a painful shoulder than the lift-off test. A positive test is useful, but combine it with the lift-off and bear-hug tests.

cards.front: Lift-off test (Gerber) — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: Specific when positive, but frequently cannot be performed. Use the belly-press test when the start position hurts.

cards.front: Speed's test — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: Only modestly accurate on its own; use it with Yergason's test and palpation of the groove.

cards.front: Yergason's test — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: Low accuracy as a single test. Combine it with Speed's test and tenderness over the groove.

cards.front: O'Brien active compression test — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: Weak on its own. Use a cluster of tests and imaging when the history strongly suggests a labral injury.

cards.front: Apprehension and relocation test — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: The apprehension itself, with relief on relocation, is the useful finding. Use the history of dislocation or subluxation first.

cards.front: Sulcus sign — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: Use it as part of the picture with the history and other laxity tests; a positive sign without symptoms is not a diagnosis.

cards.front: Load and shift test — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: Laxity is common and often not painful, so link it to symptoms and to the apprehension test before calling it instability.

cards.front: Cross-body adduction test — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: Good for AC joint pain when the joint is also tender to palpation; a negative test helps to leave the AC joint out.

cards.front: Cozen's test — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: A positive test with local tenderness is usually enough. If the pain does not behave like a tendon, look at the neck and the radial nerve.

cards.front: Mill's test — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: Useful together with Cozen's test and palpation. A positive stretch and a positive resisted test support a tendon cause.

cards.front: Resisted wrist flexion test — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: Check the ulnar nerve with Tinel's test and the elbow flexion test when there is tingling in the ring and little fingers.

cards.front: Valgus stress test (elbow) — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: Compare with the other side; a throwing history with medial pain makes the finding meaningful.

cards.front: Varus stress test (elbow) — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: Look at the history: a prior dislocation or fall on the outstretched hand makes the test far more meaningful.

cards.front: Elbow flexion test — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: Better when tingling appears early. Confirm with strength of the little finger and nerve conduction studies if symptoms persist.

cards.front: Phalen's test — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: No single test settles carpal tunnel syndrome. Combine Phalen's, Tinel's, the carpal compression test and the symptom pattern.

cards.front: Tinel's sign at the wrist — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: Moderate accuracy. It is more useful as part of a set of tests than alone.

cards.front: Carpal compression test — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: Among the more useful single tests, and quicker than Phalen's. Best used with the history, the hand diagram and thumb muscle bulk.

cards.front: Finkelstein's test — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: A positive test with tenderness over the radial styloid is reliable enough to treat; the thumb grind test separates the two causes.

cards.front: Watson scaphoid shift test — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: Relies on pain and comparison, not on a click alone. A positive test with a fall on the wrist needs imaging and hand-specialist advice.

cards.front: Froment's sign — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: Pair it with sensation of the little finger and the small hand muscles to locate an ulnar nerve problem.

cards.front: Thumb carpometacarpal grind test — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: A positive test with a bony base of the thumb, pain on pinch and an older patient is a strong picture.

cards.front: Scaphoid fracture tests — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: A cluster of three positive tests is very sensitive. Immobilise and arrange further imaging when the tests are positive, even if the first X-ray is normal.

cards.front: FABER (Patrick) test — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: Sensitive for hip pathology but not specific. Combine it with hip internal rotation range, FADIR and the history.

cards.front: FADIR test — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: High sensitivity and low specificity: a negative test makes impingement less likely, but a positive test alone does not prove it. Consider imaging only when surgery is considered.

cards.front: Hip scour (quadrant) test — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: Adds weight to the picture with FABER and FADIR; it does not tell which structure is damaged.

cards.front: Log roll test — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: Useful in a painful hip because it moves the joint with little muscle stretch; it is very sensitive for an intra-articular cause.

cards.front: Resisted straight leg raise (Stinchfield) — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: One of several hip tests to combine; groin pain on loading and on rotation together is more persuasive.

cards.front: Trendelenburg test — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: Reproducible and useful for planning gluteal strengthening; it does not tell the cause of the weakness (pain, nerve or muscle).

cards.front: Lachman test — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: The best single clinical test for the ACL; it is more accurate than the anterior drawer, particularly when the knee is acutely swollen.

cards.front: Anterior drawer test (knee) — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: Less sensitive than the Lachman test in acute injuries; use both and decide from the whole picture.

cards.front: Posterior drawer and sag sign — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: Accurate for a complete PCL tear. A positive test after a dashboard injury or a fall on a bent knee should lead to imaging.

cards.front: Pivot shift test — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: Very specific but not sensitive in the awake patient: a clear clunk is strong evidence, a negative test is not reassuring.

cards.front: McMurray test — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: Moderate accuracy. Combine it with joint line tenderness and the history (twist, locking, giving way) rather than relying on it alone.

cards.front: Thessaly test — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: Reasonable as one of several tests; a positive result with locking in the history is meaningful.

cards.front: Valgus stress test (knee) — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: Grade by the opening and the end-point; a firm end-point suggests a partial tear. Laxity when straight needs investigation of other structures.

cards.front: Varus stress test (knee) — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: Injuries to the outer side of the knee are less common but easily missed; any laxity at 0° should lead to specialist assessment.

cards.front: Patellar apprehension test — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: Strengthens the history of a patella giving way; use the findings to plan strengthening and to decide when surgery is discussed.

cards.front: Effusion tests (sweep and patellar tap) — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: Rapid swelling after an injury is a warning: ligament tears, fractures and a locked knee need early assessment.

cards.front: Ottawa knee rule — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: Very sensitive for fractures: if none of the five items is present, a fracture is unlikely. It is a decision rule, not a diagnosis.

cards.front: Anterior drawer test (ankle) — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: More accurate when repeated four to five days after the injury, once swelling and guarding have settled.

cards.front: Talar tilt (inversion stress) test — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: Use together with the anterior drawer and palpation; a severe tilt suggests both ligaments are injured.

cards.front: Squeeze test (syndesmosis) — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: High ankle sprains heal more slowly and can need protection. Repeat the test with the external rotation test, and consider imaging when weight-bearing is painful.

cards.front: External rotation (Kleiger) test — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: One of the more useful tests for a high ankle sprain; use it together with the squeeze test.

cards.front: Thompson (calf squeeze) test — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: Reliable when positive. Add a palpable gap, weakness of calf raising, and the Matles test (the foot rests in less plantarflexion when the knee is bent to 90°). Refer the same day.

cards.front: Windlass test — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: Supports a plantar fascia cause when combined with pain on the first steps in the morning and tenderness at the heel.

cards.front: Metatarsal squeeze (Mulder's click) — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: Useful with the history of burning pain in narrow shoes. Imaging is only needed if treatment fails.

cards.front: Ottawa ankle rules — how far to trust it: what must you remember?
cards.back: Highly sensitive: a negative result makes a fracture very unlikely and avoids unnecessary X-rays.
